about: The time dial. Each map names its Library of Congress picture, matched places (xy in full-resolution sheet pixels, lonlat on the real earth) and the lettering on it (spine through the letters, h their height). generator/dial_tools.py build fits a stiff bend through the matched places, writes the bent sheets to static/dial/ and fills in drawn, frame, mid and at. early holds the stops before any sheet can be laid on the earth. off: true keeps a map on record but off the dial.

early.head: A people, not yet a place
early.says: William of Rubruck rides from the Black Sea to the Mongol court at Karakorum and back, and writes of the Tartars as a people on the move, with their tents, carts and herds. The line is his road. On the world maps of his century in this atlas, the word is not yet lettered as a country.

early.head: The great wall maps do not know the name
early.says: The largest medieval world map to survive was drawn while the first reports from the Mongol courts were already in Europe, yet it carries none of them. Its northern Asia is still Scythia, with Gog and Magog walled in by Alexander. It is a round picture of the world with east at the top, so it cannot be laid on the real earth. Open it to see.

early.head: The word reaches the maps
early.says: One of the earliest maps to letter Tartaria as a region, with a note explaining it and little pictures of Tartar wagon camps, and with Gog and Magog set close by. It is engraved on a round metal plate with south at the top, so it cannot be laid on the real earth either. Open it to see.

maps.head: Three Tartarys around the Caspian
maps.title: [Carta marina navigatoria Portugallen navigationes ...] sheet 3; the running head over this sheet reads: ...IS TEMPORIBUS RECOGNITOS ET AB ANTIQUORUM TRADITIONE DIFFERENTES
maps.title_plain: Sea chart of the Portuguese voyages and of the whole known world, sheet 3 of 12: Russia, the Black Sea, the Caspian, Persia and the steppe
maps.says: This sheet letters TARTARIA three times. The largest stands on the steppe north of the Caspian Sea, over the tent of the khan, and two more east of the Caspian are tied to older country names: TARTARIA CORASINE (Khwarezm) and TARTARIA TORQVESTEN (Turkestan). North of the Sea of Azov the plain is called CAMPESTRIA TARTAR, and note after note across the sheet says that Russians, Armenians and Persians live under the Tartars.
doubts: The heading TERRA MONGAL ET QUE VERA TARTARIA DICITUR is not on this sheet. Every strip of sheet 3 was searched on close views; the heading must stand on the neighbouring sheet to the east (sheet 4), which is a different picture.

The sheet can be laid on the earth honestly in its western two thirds: the Black Sea, the Levant coast, Russia and the west and north of the Caspian come from sea charts and reports and fit to within a few hundred km. On the shared sheet it sits turned about 40 degrees, which is only the projection at this far western longitude, not a fault.

East of the Caspian there is not one place that can be matched (no Samarkand, Bukhara or Urgench on this sheet; the country there is drawn from Ptolemy with rivers and old province names). The eastern third, where TARTARIA CORASINE and TARTARIA TORQVESTEN stand, is therefore carried along by the western fit and its position on the earth is only a rough guide.

The Caspian is drawn as an oval lying east to west, as on the old sea charts, so its true north-south shape cannot be matched; the points on it (Volga delta, Kura mouth, Ural mouth, south shore) pull against each other.

Derbent could not be found by name on the west shore of the Caspian. Astrakhan is lettered only as agitarcam in the list of names at the Volga delta, with no sign of its own. CASANA (Kazan) is lettered as a country near the Don, with no town sign, and was not used.
Sarai is read from the town lettered Sala ciuit. on the Volga; the river name dayr fl. is read as the Yaik (Ural); Grassan is read as Kashan. All three are marked not sure.
CAMPESTRIA TARTAR: the second line reads TAR TAR and seems cut short (for Tartarorum or Tartarie).
A small name east of the Sea of Azov reads Tacaria over Tarmacho (about x 2190, y 2985). It may be a slip for Tartaria but it is lettered with a c, so it is not recorded as a Tartary label.

Many of the written notes on the sheet name the Tartars (sub mandato Tartarorum, sub dominio Tartarorum, sub tributo tartarorum, the boxed note beginning Tartari semper morantur in campis). These are text blocks and are not recorded as labels.
The title given is the running head printed over this sheet; the map's main title stands on another sheet.

Lands: the sheet draws no border for any Tartary name. A dotted line runs from the Hyperborei montes down to the north shore of the Caspian near dayr fl., just east of the last letter of TARTARIA and of CVMANIE; it is taken as the east side of TARTARIA, but the sheet does not say whether it is a border or a road.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet draws no border for this name, so the ring is a reading of the lettering and of the rivers and mountains around it. North: the upper Volga, then the foot of the Hyperborei montes. East: a dotted line the sheet draws from those mountains down towards the Caspian, just past the last letter; the sheet does not say what the line is. South: east of the Volga the ring stops halfway to the equally large name CVMANIE, which puts it through the boxed note on how the Tartars live; west of the Volga it runs down the river to its delta and along the top of the Caucasus chain, because the note under the khan's tent says his host goes up to the mountains in summer and down to the sea in winter. West: the Don (tanais) where it loops nearest, then the east face of the mountain chain that runs north to the Volga. The smaller names BVLGARIA MAGNA and NAGAI and the khan's tent fall inside.

lands.name: CAMPESTRIA TARTAR
lands.note: The sheet draws no border for this name; the ring is the small plain the two lines of lettering fill. North: a line just over the lettering, under the name CREMANI and the tent of the Crimean khan, which are left outside. East: the Don (la tana) down to its mouth. South: the shore of the Sea of Azov as the sheet draws it. West: the small river that runs to the sea just before the first letter.

lands.name: TARTARIA CORASINE
lands.note: The sheet draws no border for this name; the words Que Sogdiana after it tie it to Ptolemy's Sogdiana, the land between the two great rivers, and the ring follows them. North: the river lettered iaxartes fl. from its mouth to its bend. East: the same river where it turns south along the foot of the eastern range, then a short cut across the mountains. South: the river that runs east from the lake, the lake, and the river lettered oxias fl. down to the Caspian (hidden for a stretch under the tent of NOY). West: the Caspian shore between the two river mouths; the lettering itself starts well east of the shore, so this western end is the least sure part.

lands.name: TARTARIA TORQVESTEN
lands.note: The sheet draws no border for this name. Its three lines are spread over two mountain chains, with the words Que Bactriana, Que et Aria and Que paropanisus beside them, so the ring takes in all the ground the letters cross. North: the river oxias fl., the lake and the river running east from it (the same line as the south side of TARTARIA CORASINE). East: the foot of the range east of TAR TA, then the foot of the chain north of the letters QVEST, then the edge of the sheet. South: the mountain chain that parts it from Que Arachosia, and further west the chain that parts it from the Persian empire and SOPHI REX. West: a river running south from the oxias, past the mountains beside the tent of NOY.

maps.head: One word, letter by letter, across the steppe
maps.title: RVSSIAE, MOSCOVIAE ET TARTARIAE DESCRIPTIO. Auctore Antonio Ienkensono Anglo, edita Londini Anno 1562 & dedicata illustriss. D. Henrico Sydneo Wallie presidi.
maps.title_plain: A description of Russia, Muscovy and Tartary, by Anthony Jenkinson, Englishman, published at London in 1562 and dedicated to Sir Henry Sidney, Lord President of Wales
maps.says: The word TARTARIA is lettered once, in big letters spread one by one across the open steppe from the Don and lower Volga eastward past the Yaik toward the country above Tashkent. It is not divided into parts; smaller names such as Nagaia, Cassacki, Turkmen and Kirges sit inside and around it, and the far north is given to the Samoyeds instead. A note beside Samarkand calls that city the former capital of all Tartary.
doubts: This is a 1914 black and white Russian reproduction that follows Ortelius's 1570 reduced plate, not the 1562 London sheet; fine lettering is blurred in places.

The word also appears inside two text notes (Samarkand 'olim totius Tartariae metropolis' and Little Khorasan taken 'adiuvantibus Tartaris 1558') and in the title; these are text blocks and are not recorded as labels.

The also names CASSACKI and TVRKMEN are broken over three and two lines and are given one entry per line. BOGHAR, SHAMARGHAN, KIRGES, TASKENT, MHOGOL, COLMACK, BAIDA and MOLGOMZAIA are also lettered as region names but left out to keep to eight entries.
The Vardo and Kola spots are read from a dark, crowded coast and may be 20 to 30 pixels off.
The Ob, Sibir, Tashkent and Kashgar came from hearsay and sit far from their true places; the Caspian is drawn wider east to west than north to south, so its shore towns fit badly.
The spine of the TARTARIA label was moved onto the centres of the eight letters as read at full size; several of the earlier spots were 50 to 110 pixels off along the line. The reading is unchanged.

The last A of TARTARIA is a small letter set straight under the KI of CASSACKI and above the I. It is taken as the end of TARTARIA, since the word would otherwise stop at TARTARI, but it could be read with the letters above it.

The land ring for TARTARIA rests on the lettering alone. Its north side east of the Samara, its east end and the turn round the second R are lines of judgment; the other sides borrow rivers, the Caspian shore and the dotted limits of Astracan, of the Turkmen country and of Bukhara and Tashkent.
The dotted line from the north-east corner of the Caspian toward the second R is taken as the north limit of the Turkmen country; it stops short just before the R, so the R sits at its open end.

The ring is kept modest. The note at Samarkand calls that city the former capital of all Tartary, so the mapmaker's idea of Tartary reached further south-east than the ring, but the provinces there (BOGHAR, SHAMARGHAN, TASKENT) are closed off by their own dotted lines and are left out.
CRIMEA is lettered west of the first T as a name of the lower rank and is left outside the ring; ASTRACAN has its own dotted limit and is left outside too.
The also names TVRK and MEN sit at about x 3270 to 3470, y 2900 and x 3055 to 3225, y 3300 on the sheet; their recorded spines are 50 to 85 pixels off and were not changed in this pass.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet draws no limit of its own for TARTARIA and this black and white copy has no colour, so the ring is the ground the spread letters cover, carried out to the nearest rivers and dotted lines. North: the stream joining the Ploga and Ivan lakes under the name MORDVA, then the Volga up to the Samara, the Samara to its head, and from there a straight line of my own about halfway between TARTARIA and TVMEN, with NAGAIA left inside. East: the river that runs down from the Kitaia lake, then a line of my own passing just under the KI of CASSACKI and stopping at the picture of the kneeling Kirghiz, a little past the last letters. South: the engraved dotted line that closes the Bukhara and Tashkent country on the north, a line of my own round the foot of the second R, the engraved dotted line that runs from there south-west to the river at the north-east corner of the Caspian with TVRK lettered below it, the north shore of the Caspian, the engraved dotted line round the east of ASTRACAN, and the lower Don below the first T. West: the Sosna river, which lies about halfway between the first T and the name CRIMEA. The dotted lines used are the limits of neighbouring provinces, not of Tartaria itself.

maps.sheet: Tartary, or the kingdom of the Great Khan
maps.head: The Great Khan's whole realm under one word
maps.title: TARTARIAE SIVE MAGNI CHAMI REGNI typus
maps.title_plain: Map of Tartary, or the kingdom of the Great Khan
maps.says: Ortelius letters TARTARIA once, in large capitals across the steppe north-east of the Caspian, and adds in small script that it takes in Asiatic Sarmatia and both Scythias of the ancient writers. He does not divide it into Great, Little or Chinese Tartary; the rest of the country is filled with the names of hordes and with Marco Polo's kingdoms such as Tangut, Camul, Tenduc and Cathay, all of them, by the title and the note in the lower cartouche, under the Great Khan.
doubts: The word Tartary also occurs inside blocks of text, which were not recorded as labels: the title cartouche (TARTARIAE SIVE MAGNI CHAMI REGNI typus), the lower left cartouche ('Continet hec tabula oem Tartariam'), the note by the Great Khan's tent ('lingua Tartarorum') and the Altai note ('oes Tartarie imperatores').
A town on the China coast is lettered Tartaho (about 3550,3730); it is a town name, not the word Tartary, and was not recorded.

The interior east of Samarkand and the whole north-east coast (Scythicum prom., Tabin, Arsareth, the Strait of Anian) are legend, so nothing fixes the sheet there; the fit rests on the Black Sea, Caspian, the Russian north coast to the Ob, the China coast and Japan.
No fitting place could be found in the south-west and south (Persia and India are covered by a cartouche and blank lettering), so that side of the sheet is held only by Tabriz, Merv and Termez.
Moscow and Bukhara are not on this sheet (it begins east of Moscow and uses Gastaldi's names beyond the Caspian), and Canton lies off the bottom edge; Korea and Novaya Zemlya are not drawn.
The Caspian is drawn as an east to west oval and Hangzhou (Quinsai) far north of Ningbo, so those places land far off however the sheet is laid; they are true identities and were kept.
Merv, Termez and Margilan are read from Gastaldi-style names (Maru, Terment, Merglan) and marked not sure.
The stub's 'Siberia' pin at 105E 61N was changed to the town of Sibir near Tobolsk, which is what the symbol stands for.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet draws no boundary for this name: there is no dotted line anywhere, and the hand colour is only a pink wash along every coast of Asia (yellow for America), not a limit between countries. The ring is therefore the ground the sheet's own words give to 'Tartary or the kingdom of the Great Khan': the lower left cartouche says his empire is bounded by the river Ob, lake Kataia, the river Volga, the Caspian Sea, the river Chesel, Mount Ussonte, the region of Thebet, the river Caromoran and the Ocean, and the ring follows those features as they are engraved. West: the Volga from its mouth up past Astracan to Bulgar and Casan and its branch to Corelniz, then the short dotted line to Themisbi (the only dotted line on the sheet, more likely a portage than a border) and the river to Kytaia lacus; EVROPAE PARS, ZVIRIA, GEORGIANI and DVCIS MOSCOVIAE CONFINIA lie outside. North: the west shore of Kytaia lacus, the river lettered Oby fl. to its mouth, then the engraved Arctic coast round the long inlet beside Vaigatz and round Scythicum prom. East: the engraved coast of the Scythian Ocean and the Strait of Anian, round the gulf below Chiorsa and round Arsareth and Tabin, down the coast of Quinci and Xanton to the mouth of the river that carries the name Caromoran; Japan and the islands are left out (the note beside Japan says the Great Khan attacked it in vain). South: up that river (lettered Quanzu near the sea, Caromoran fl. above) to Guian lake, by the Mesu stream and the river past Baicundel and the town of Thebet, then a judged line between CAINDV and THEBET and between ERGIMVL and CARAZAN to the east end of the Monte Vssonte chain, along its crest, then a judged line north to the head of the stream at Chuche and down that stream and the trunk of the Chesel to the Caspian; CHINA, CHEQVAN, MOIN, THEBET, CARAZAN, PARS INDIAE, TACALISTAN, SIM, HAND, SAMARCHAND, ZAGATAI and REGNI PERSIAE CONFINIA lie outside, CATAIO, MANGI, TANGVT, CAMVL, TVRCHESTAN and MAVRENAHER inside. Southwest corner: the east and north shore of the Caspian from the Chesel mouth to the Volga mouth. Graded loose because the limit is read from words and from rivers and mountains, not from a drawn border, because the two links on the south side and the choice of Chesel branch are judgement, and because the cartouche speaks of 'all Tartary with the rest of eastern Asia that obeys the Great Khan', so the word TARTARIA itself may have been meant for less than this ring.

maps.says: Arnoldi letters TARTARIA once, in the largest capitals on the sheet, spread in two groups of letters (TAR and TARIA) across the north of Asia from east of the Ob to a gulf of the northern sea. He draws no border round it and does not split it into Great, Little or Chinese Tartary. A long Italian note between the two groups of letters describes the land of the Tartars as dry, windy, short of towns and mostly Muslim. Around the name he letters hordes in the north, Turchestan, Maurenaher and Zagatai towards the Caspian Sea, and Marco Polo's Bargu, Tangut, Cataio and Mangi towards China, with Moscovia, Russia, Casan and Astracan on the west.
doubts: The sheet as scanned carries no date, no maker's name and no publisher's line that could be found; the only title is ASIA in the cartouche. The names Arnoldo di Arnoldi and Matteo Florimi of Siena and the date of about 1600 come from the Library of Congress catalogue, which gives the imprint in brackets and the date as 1600 with a question mark. The catalogue also says the lower left and upper left corners of the margin are cut away on this copy.

The word Tartar also stands in a text note that was not marked as a label: 'La Regione de Tartari sarebbe quasi tutto sterile, se l'acque de fiumi, che pur vi sono rari, non la bagnassero ...', ending 'I suoi popoli osservano per il piu la fede Maumetana' (about 2460 to 3350 across, 1340 to 1650 down). It says the land of the Tartars would be almost barren but for its few rivers, is beaten by strong winds and frightful summer thunder, has few towns, and that its peoples mostly keep the Muslim faith.

TARTARIA is one name lettered in two groups, TAR (about 2190 to 2440 across) and TARIA (about 3445 to 3875 across), with the note in the gap of about 1000 pixels between them. It was recorded as two labels with the same reading. The first T has a long flourish and could be mistaken for another letter.

No other lettering with Tartar in it was found. There is no Little Tartary north of the Black Sea (the sheet shows Caffa, Tana and Circassi there without the word), no Tartar sea and no Tartar horde by name. The cartouche text does not use the word.

The sheet is drawn on a heart-shaped kind of projection with the pole near the top middle, so north points to the right at the Black Sea and to the left at Japan. The bend has to turn the two sides of the sheet in opposite ways.

The whole north-east (Scitycum prom., Tabor, Belgian, Argon, Arsareth, Tabin prom., and Quinsai set on the far north-east coast) is drawn from legend and from Marco Polo, and Korea, Novaya Zemlya and the White Sea are not on the sheet. Nothing real fixes the sheet between the Ob and Japan north of Nanjing, which is exactly where the second half of the name TARTARIA lies, so its place on today's earth is only a rough carry-over.

Inner Asia east of Samarkand is Marco Polo's (Cascar, Coton, Lop, Camul, Succuir, Campion, Caracoran, Xandu, Cambalu); those places were recorded and left out of the fit. Kabul, Lahore, Samarkand, Bukhara and Termez are the only inner places used; Termez (Terment) is not a sure reading.
Vaigatz is drawn as a tiny island right at the mouth of the Ob. It was left out of the fit because it sits on top of the Ob mouth point; the Ob itself runs out of the legendary lake Kitaia Lacus.

The Caspian Sea is drawn as an oval lying east to west in the old manner, and the Sea of Azov is small and turned, so Azov, Derbent and the Yaik mouth land some way off. Delhi (Delli) is drawn far south of Lahore beside Orissa. These are the mapmaker's errors and were kept.

Two towns are lettered Multan (Multan near Cabul and Moltan on the Indus); it was not clear which is meant, so neither was used. Tascan (taken as Tashkent) is drawn south-east of Samarkand and was left out. A town on the China coast lettered Cliche or Chiche may be Chincheo; it was left out.
Sinop (Ginopoli) and the Indus delta port Diul are less sure matches; both were used in the fit and are marked not sure.

The land ring for TARTARIA is a judgement from the lettering only. Its east side is a straight judged line, and its south side follows the first rivers below the letters, which leaves Tangut and Cataio outside although a reader of 1600 might well have counted them as Tartary. A wider reading would add them; a narrower one would drop Turchestan and Maurenaher.
The west side of the ring follows the Yaick, the lake Kitaia Lacus and the Ob. Casan, Obdora and Astracan were left outside as the Muscovite side, but the sheet draws no line to say so.
Besides the title cartouche (cut out as a hole), three text notes and several sea monsters and ships stand in the sea; they were not cut out.
uncertain: This copy shows no date and no maker's name. Arnoldi, Florimi of Siena and the date of about 1600 come from the Library of Congress catalogue.
The sheet draws no border round Tartary and has no colour. The outline shown is a reading of where the letters lie, carried to the nearest coast and rivers.
The outline leaves Tangut and Cathay outside. A reader in 1600 might have counted them as part of Tartary; the sheet does not say.
The far north-east of the sheet is drawn from legend and from Marco Polo, with no real places to pin it down. The second half of the name lies there, so its place on the modern map is rough.
The word Tartar also appears in a long note on the sheet about the land of the Tartars. It is not marked as a label.
The Caspian Sea, the Sea of Azov and Delhi are badly placed on the sheet itself, so they land far from their true spots.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet is not coloured and draws no boundary line, so this ring is a reading of the lettering, carried out to the nearest natural limits the sheet shows. North: the coast of the northern sea (Mare Scythicum overo di Tabin) from the mouth of the Ob, round the gulf east of it, past Scitycum prom. and Insula falconum to the gulf below Tabor; the ring steps across the mouth of the long inlet that runs down between the R and the I of the name. East: a judged straight line from that gulf south to the town of Rasalcan, drawn just beyond the last letter and the name Belgian, and well short of Argon, Arsareth and Mangi; nothing on the sheet marks this side. South: the first water line below the lettering, that is the river from Rasalcan and Iaurin past Palignan to the lake at Xandu, the river from there west to the lake below Caracoran, a judged line past the north side of the three lakes above the Deserto di Lop to the town of Lop, then the river lettered Chesel fl. west to the Caspian Sea. Tangut, Cataio (with Cambalu), Zagatai and Samarcand stay outside; Turchestan, Maurenaher, Bargu, Tabor, Belgian, Caracoran, Monte di Althay and the long note on the land of the Tartars lie inside. West: the Caspian shore north to the mouth of the Yaick, up the Yaick, a judged line to the lake called Kitaia Lacus, round its west shore and down the Ob to the sea. The hordes lettered between the Yaick and the Ob gulf (Baschirdorum, Zibierairorum, Chiesanorum, Mecritorum, Vsezucanorum, Ciremissorum, Turbonum) lie inside; Astracan, Casan, Obdora, RVSSIA and MOSCOVIA stay outside.

maps.title_plain: Asia with the adjoining islands described, with the dress of the people and the towns of importance, all newly enlarged by John Speed, 1626
maps.says: Speed letters TARTARIA in large spaced capitals across the country between the Volga and the Ob, running up from north of the Caspian Sea. The word comes back three more times: as a tribe (Kaski Tartari) in the steppe below it, as a town called Tartar in the empty far north-east, and on the water as The Tartarian Sea along the whole Arctic coast. A note beside the Great Wall says it was built against sudden inroads of the Tartars, and one of the costume figures in the border is labelled Tartarian.
doubts: The tribe name under TARTARIA has a meridian line through its third letter; it is read here as 'Kaski Tartari' (long s, probably the Kazakhs), which earlier notes gave as 'Kalbi Tartari'. 'Kalki' is also possible.

The note on the Great Wall ('...against the suddaine in fall of ye Tartars on this side', about x 4350-4720, y 2040-2090) and the border figure lettered TARTARIAN (lower right) hold the word but are a text note and border decoration, so they are not recorded as labels.
North-east Asia is drawn by guess (Mongul, Tenduc, Tartar, a coast running to a strait with America), so nothing fixes the fit there beyond Beijing and northern Japan.
The Caspian is the old east-west oval, and Samarkand is set far east; both are kept as true places the mapmaker misplaced.
The picture is a photograph of an open book with a gutter near x 3600 and some page curve, and the plate edge is slightly out of square (corners near 619,476; 6630,451; 6644,5120; 649,5148).
Mogadishu and Macao town marks are uncertain to a few tens of pixels.

No limit of TARTARIA is engraved or coloured. The land ring is loose: its west side (Volga, Cazan to Weliki Perm, the hills to the Pechora) and its east side (the river from the Arctic inlet at Colmak to Annibi Lake and Kithai Lake) are judged, and a wider reading that takes in all of north Asia to the Great Wall is possible.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet draws no boundary line and has no colour, so this ring is a reading of the lettering, carried out to the nearest natural limits the sheet shows. North: the Arctic coast (the Tartarian Sea) from the Pechora mouth past the Ob mouth to the inlet between Colmak and Cavona. East: the river that runs from that inlet down to Annibi Lake, then a short judged line to Kithai Lake, where the Ob rises; this is the first water line beyond the last letter. South: the Sur river from Kithai Lake to Taskent, a short judged line to the river at Cotan and Calha, that river west to the Caspian, then the north shore of the Caspian to the Volga delta; this lies about halfway to PERSIA, and Zagathay stays outside. West: the Volga from its delta up to Cazan, the river from Cazan to Weliki Perm, then a judged line north along the west foot of the hills lettered weliki poiassa and Camen to the Pechora river and down it to the sea; the only name of equal rank on this side is PART OF EUROPA far to the west. Inside lie the lower-rank names Nagaia horda, Kalmucki, Kaski Tartari, Tumen, Sibier, Lucomoria, Iougoria, Condora, Obdora, SAMOIEDA, BAIDA, Molgomzaia, Colmak, Karkithay and Turch.

maps.head: One word from the Volga to Cathay
maps.by: Willem Blaeu, published by Nicolaes Visscher
maps.title: NOVA ET EXACTA ASIÆ GEOGRAPHICA DESCRIPTIO, auct: G: I: Blaeu
maps.title_plain: A new and exact geographical description of Asia, by Willem Janszoon Blaeu
maps.says: Blaeu letters TARTARIA once, in the largest capitals on the land, one letter at a time from west of the Volga across the Ob to the kingdom of Tangut, with no border line round it. Under it he names Tartar peoples (the Kazakh Tartars and the Kalmuks, "that is, long-haired Tartars"), a Chagatai Tartary by Bukhara, and north of the Black Sea "Crimea, or Perekop Tartary". There is no Siberia as a country, only the town Sibier on the Ob; the north is RUSSIA, SAMOIEDA, Lucomorye and Yugra, and the far east is filled with Marco Polo's names (Tangut, Tenduc, Mongul, Cathay with Cambalu) and a town and river called Tartar. A note on the Great Wall says it was built against the raids of the Tartars, and the printed text in the border calls the country "the empire of the Great Cham, or Tartary".
doubts: The date is not printed on the sheet. The privilege in the lower right cartouche ends 'datae Hagae Comitis die 5 Augusti' with no year that can be read on this copy, and the imprint at the foot of the map reads only '[N] Visscher excudit'. The year 1657 is the Library of Congress catalogue's guess ('[1657?]') for Visscher's issue; Blaeu first published this wall map about 1608.

The title strip over the map reads 'NOVA ET EXACTA ASIÆ GEOGRAPHICA DESCRIPTIO, auct: G: I: Blaeu'. The catalogue gives a different title, 'Nova et acurata totius Asiae tabula'. The cartouche inside the map says only ASIA.
The copy is browned and worn, with patches of lost surface and bare linen; small lettering is faint in places.
ZAGATAY Tart.: one capital between T and Y is worn, and 'Tart.' is cut short, so it may mean Tartaria or Tartari.
The river name beside the town Tartar reads '...rta flu.'; the first letters are worn and it is taken as 'Tarta flu.' from the same name on sister maps.

The word also stands in notes that are not marked as labels: 'Murus quadringentarum leucarum ... contra Tartarorum ab hac parte eruptiones, extructus' on the Great Wall (about x 12600 to 13200, y 2950 to 3350); 'Castrum in quo presidia collocarat Vutcham contra irruptionem Tartarorum' (about x 13000, y 1700); the note on the bronze trumpeters 'quos verisimile est Tartaros in perpetuam vindicatae libertatis memoriam ... posuisse' (about x 12700, y 1000 to 1200); 'Care desertum per quod in Chathaium eunt ac redeunt Tartari' (about x 10700, y 3500); and a note near Carli of which only '...tarorum sepulchra sunt' can be read.

In the border, a costume picture on the right is lettered TARTARI, and the French text beside it begins 'La troisieme partie de l'Asie est l'Empire du Grand Cham ou Tartarie' and goes on to name la Tartarie Deserte, the Lesser Tartary facing Europe, Zagatar, Cataio and Tangut. These are outside the map and are not marked.

North-east Asia is drawn by guess: the Arctic coast east of the Ob, the island Tazata, the Strait of Anian and all the towns there come from Marco Polo and older maps. Nothing fixes the fit there beyond Beijing, Korea and Japan, so where the east end of TARTARIA falls on the real earth is loose.
Cambalu (Marco Polo's Beijing, drawn as a separate city in Cathay), Carocoran, Camul, the town Tartar and Taskent (lettered twice, east of Kashgar) were kept out of the fit.

Places that stay far off because the sheet itself is wrong there: Beijing (C. Paquin), set much too far north and west; the north tip of Japan; Delhi (Delli), set far south near Orissa; Kandahar and Kabul; Kashgar; Isfahan; and the Caspian, drawn as an oval lying east and west with Bukhara close to its shore.
Korea is drawn as a long island (COREA INSULA); its south-west tip was matched to the cape lettered Punta dos ladrones.
The town marks used for Weliki Perm (taken as Cherdyn), Pitzora (taken as Pustozersk), Cola and Masulipata are small and a little uncertain.

The sheet draws no border round TARTARIA. The ring is my reading: Arctic coast, Pacific coast, the Great Wall, the Oxus, the Caspian and the Ob, with judged lines between. The line from the west end of the Wall to the Oxus and the line between the Volga and the Ob are the weakest parts.
SAMOIEDA is lettered across the lower Ob, so its last letters fall inside the TARTARIA ring; the Ob was still taken as the limit there because RUSSIA is lettered wholly west of it.

The holes cut out are the ASIA cartouche with its two figures (top left), the inset of the south polar lands (right), the distance diagram and its text (left), the note cartouche in the Indian Ocean and the privilege cartouche (bottom right); their outlines are approximate.
uncertain: The date is not printed on the sheet. About 1657 is the Library of Congress's estimate for this issue by Nicolaes Visscher; Blaeu first made the map about fifty years earlier.

The sheet draws no border round TARTARIA, so its outline here is judged from the lettering and the nearest coasts, rivers and the Great Wall. The stretch from the Wall to the Oxus river and the stretch between the Volga and the Ob are the least certain.

North-east Asia is drawn by guess from Marco Polo and older maps (Tenduc, Cathay with Cambalu, a town called Tartar, the Strait of Anian), so the east end of TARTARIA cannot be placed firmly on the real earth.
ZAGATAY Tart. is cut short on the sheet, so it may mean a country (Tartaria) or a people (Tartari).
Several notes on the map and the printed text and a costume picture in the border also use the word; they were read but not marked.
Some true places sit far from where they belong because the mapmaker misplaced them: Beijing, Delhi, Kashgar, northern Japan and the east shore of the Caspian.

lands.name: TARTARIA
lands.note: The sheet draws no boundary line round TARTARIA and the copy has no colour on the land, so this ring is a reading of the lettering, carried out to the nearest natural limits the sheet shows. North: the Arctic coast as drawn, from the mouth of the Ob east past the gulf with the island Tazata to the north-east corner by Bargu. East: the coast on the Strait of Anian down to where the mountains behind the Great Wall reach the sea; Tenduc, Ung, Mongul and Cathay with Cambalu are lower-rank names and stay inside. South: the Great Wall of China (lettered as built against the Tartars) to its west end, then a judged line south-west past Carcham and Taskent to the long mountain chain, leaving Carazan and Sim Mau outside; then a judged line west to the lake Babacamber and along the Oxus river to the south-east corner of the Caspian, so that Samarchand, Maurenaher, Buccara and Zagatay stay inside and PERSIA and INDIA stay outside. West: the east and north shores of the Caspian to Astracan, a judged line north-west between the Volga and the Don to take in the first letter T, then north of Bulgaria and south of Cazan and Permia (about halfway to the last letter of RUSSIA) to the Ob near Sibier, and down the Ob to the sea. Inside lie the lower-rank names Nagaia Horda, Kalmucki, Kasakki Tartari, Zagatay, Tumen, Ioughoria, Lucomorye, Baida, Colmak, Kithaisko, Karakithay, Turchestan, Tanguth, Mongul, Bargu and Cathay.

maps.head: Great Tartary, from the Ob to the Pacific
maps.title: MAGNÆ TARTARIÆ, MAGNI MOGOLIS IMPERII, IAPONIÆ et CHINÆ, Nova Descriptio
maps.title_plain: A new description of Great Tartary, the Empire of the Great Mogul, Japan and China
maps.says: The words TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary, are spread one letter at a time across the whole of inner Asia, from the river Ob to the Pacific coast and from the Arctic shore down to the Great Wall of China. Inside that space the sheet names many separate peoples and kingdoms, among them the Kazakh Tartars, Chagatai, Turkestan, the Mongols, Cathay and Tangut, and the Arctic sea above is called the Tartar Sea. Siberia is only a small name by the Ob, and the far north-east is filled with names from Marco Polo and from legend, such as Magog and a town and river called Tartar.
doubts: Three short Latin notes on the map body also use the word and are not recorded as labels: 'Castrum contra irruptionem Tartarorum' near 6800,3045, 'eunt ac redeunt Tartari' near 3400,3280, and 'Regnum Tartariae Sepulchra sunt' near 5600,3240, besides the note on the trumpeters near 6700,2330.
'Tart.' after ZACATAY is cut short on the sheet, so it may mean Tartaria or Tartari.

North of China and east of the Ob almost nothing on the sheet is real: the Arctic and north-east coasts are guesses, there is no Baikal, Aral or Amur, and the towns come from Marco Polo. The fit there rests on the Ob and Yenisei mouths and on the Dutch survey of Yezo and Sakhalin at the east edge, so the place of the TARTARIA lettering on the earth is loose.
The Volga mouth and Astrakhan fall off the left edge, so the west side is held by the Ural river mouth, Samara, Saratov and Bolgar.
Tashkent is lettered far to the east of Samarkand and is kept out of the fit.
Two places stay flagged after a second look because the sheet itself is wrong there: Verkhoturye (about 1000 km off) and the south-east corner of the Caspian (about 500 km off).

Land of TARTARIA MAGNA: the sheet draws no line labelled as the limit of Tartary itself. The ring uses the dashed limits engraved for Russia, Persia, the Mogul empire, China and Corea, plus the Great Wall and the coasts, and takes everything left between them as Great Tartary.

A narrow wedge on the upper Croceus (Yellow) river, between the dashed west limit of China and the dashed east limit of the Mogul lands, belongs to neither on the sheet and was kept inside Great Tartary.
ZACATAY Tart. gets no land: a dotted line runs across its lettering rather than round it. Sumongul al: Tartar. gets no land: it sits among river cells with no boundary line of its own.
The island Tazata off the Arctic coast is left out of the land.

lands.name: TARTARIA MAGNA
lands.note: The sheet has no colour, so the ring follows the engraved dashed boundary lines of the neighbouring empires and the coasts. North: the Arctic coast as drawn, from the mouth of the Peisida river east to the north-east corner, leaving out the island called Tazata. East: the Pacific coast down to the short dashed line that cuts off Corea. South: that dashed line, then the Great Wall of China westward, then the dashed limit of China beyond the west end of the Wall and down its west side, then the dashed limit of the Mogul empire (past Gor, along the Dalanguer mountains and round the lake by Escalcand), then the dashed limit of Persia along the Abbia river and the Oxus to the Caspian. West: the east shore of the Caspian up to the Iaick, then the dashed limit of Russia north-east past the Iaick and the Ob, west of lake Kithaika, to the Arctic coast. Tibet, Turkestan, Samarkand and Bukhara fall inside. Between the dashed limits of China and of the Mogul lands a narrow wedge on the upper Croceus (Yellow) river is left to neither, and it is kept inside the ring. The lower line of the name, MAGNA, and the title, which lists only Great Tartary, the Mogul empire, Japan and China, agree with these limits.

maps.head: One Great Tartary, split by ruler
maps.title: L'Asie, dressée sur les observations de l'Academie Royale des Sciences et quelques autres, et sur les memoires les plus recens. Par G. de l'Isle Geographe. A Paris, chéz l'Auteur sur le Quai de l'Horloge, avec Privilege du Roy pour 20. ans, 1700.
maps.title_plain: Asia, drawn from the observations of the Royal Academy of Sciences and some others, and from the most recent accounts, by G. Delisle, geographer. Paris, at the author's house on the Quai de l'Horloge, with the King's privilege for 20 years, 1700
maps.says: Delisle letters GRANDE TARTARIE once, in the largest capitals of inner Asia, in a single line from the Volga to the Amur, and then splits that ground by who rules it. Engraved dotted lines mark off TARTARIE MOSCOVITE across the north from the White Sea to the Yenisei and Lake Baikal, TARTARIE INDEPENDANTE from the Caspian to the Mongols (its line also takes in the kingdoms of Tibet), and TARTARIE CHINOISE north of the Great Wall, which carries TARTARIE OCCIDENTALE and TARTARIE OR.LE (Orientale) inside it. PETITE TARTARIE stands apart on the steppe north of the Black Sea, with the Crimea. Inside these he letters peoples and countries of their own, such as SIBERIE, the Samoyeds, Ostyaks, Tungus and Yakuts, the Kalmyks, Uzbeks, TURQUESTAN and the Mongols, and no people on the sheet is called Tartars.
doubts: The date 1700 is printed in the title cartouche: 'Avec Privilege du Roy pour 20. ans 1700'. The address in the same cartouche is the Quai de l'Horloge. As far as I know Delisle only moved to that quay some years after 1700 (his first maps of 1700 give the Rue des Canettes), so this copy is probably a later printing of the plate that kept the 1700 date. That rests on my own knowledge of his addresses and was not checked against a reference here.

The cartouche picture is signed 'N. Guerard Inv. et fecit'. The word Tartarie does not appear in the title, in the Avertissement block at lower left, or in the scale table. No lettering with 'Tartares' (a people) was found anywhere on the sheet after reading it strip by strip; the Nogais by Astrakhan are lettered NOGAIS only.

GRANDE TARTARIE has no limit of its own on the sheet. Its ring is the Muscovite, Independent and Chinese parts together, carried to the Arctic and Pacific coast, so it also takes in the land of Jelmer, the Yakut country and the plain of Bargu, which the engraved lines keep out of Muscovite Tartary. Novaya Zemlya is drawn joined to the mainland and was cut off by a judged line near the river mouth at Port de la glace.

The second T of TARTARIE in GRANDE TARTARIE, near Selenginsk, is half lost under the border colour; it looks like an I with a small 'AT' engraved beside it. The spine point for it is set from the spacing of the letters.

TARTARIE MOSCOVITE: the ring is the whole pink compartment inside the engraved dotted line. It reaches west of the Urals to the Mezen, Viatka, Kazan, Astrakhan and Circassia, far beyond the lettering, which runs only from Viatka to the Lena country. The Yakut country (yellow) and the plain of Bargu (green, with the note 'occupée par les Moscovites') lie outside that line and are left out, though the sheet itself says the Muscovites hold the second.

TARTARIE INDEPENDANTE: the engraved outer line and the green wash take in Kashgar and all the kingdoms of Tibet down to Lassa. The name is lettered only across the Kalmyk and Turkestan country. Whether Delisle meant Tibet to count as Independent Tartary, or only left it without a line of its own, the sheet does not say.

The split between TARTARIE OCCIDENTALE and TARTARIE OR.LE is taken along the engraved dotted line from the Argun past the Dauri to the east end of the Great Wall. The sheet does not label that line. The first word of TARTARIE OCCIDENTALE is lettered outside Chinese Tartary, on the green beside Tibet, and the first letters of TARTARIE OR.LE stand on the pink of the Muscovite side near Nerchinsk.

Hand colour and engraved lines agree on this copy nearly everywhere; the rings follow the engraved dotted or dashed lines, read at full size on most sides and at reduced size along parts of the Persian and Indian borders.

North-east Asia is drawn by hearsay. The Lena reaches the sea in a 'Golfe de Len' about ten degrees too far south, Yakutsk sits beside it, and the Okhota and Uda rivers are drawn almost side by side. These places are certain but fit badly (Lena mouth about 1300 km, Yakutsk about 940 km, Uda mouth about 630 km when left out). A mountain spur (Noss chaine de Montagne) runs off to the north-east with the note that nobody yet knows where it ends or whether it joins another continent. No Kamchatka is drawn.
The mouth of the Amur is drawn hard against the land of Yeço with only a narrow strait between, so the Amur mouth (about 850 km off) and Matsumae (about 600 km off) fit badly.

Lake Baikal is drawn small with Irkutsk at its north end, and Krasnoyarsk (Kramosar) and Tomsk (Tomo) are crowded against it; Tomsk is set south of Krasnoyarsk in the Kirghiz country, about 600 km out. Tomo is taken to be Tomsk from the name; that reading is likely but not certain.
Lassa is drawn well east of where Lhasa is (about 430 km off when left out). An earlier point for it had been set by mistake on the name Tache Linbou and was moved to the town sign marked Lassa.

Campion is Marco Polo's name for Ganzhou (Zhangye). The sheet shows it as a town north-east of Cancheou, which is the same place under its Chinese name, so Campion is left out of the fit and Cancheou is used. Yarchan (Yarkand) is drawn north of Casgar (Kashgar), the wrong way round, and is left out of the fit; Kashgar itself fits about 500 km off.

Some of the other big names were read from spread letters that cross rivers and each other: SAMOGEDES and TONGUSI run one after the other down the same slanting line east of the Ob, and I took them as two names; USBECS is spread across Bukhara and Balkh. Their outlines are approximate.
The south and east of the sheet (Arabia, India, the islands, the Pacific) were read at reduced size; no Tartary lettering is expected or was seen there.
uncertain: The sheet is dated 1700, but the address on it (Quai de l'Horloge) suggests this copy was printed some years later from the same plate.
Great Tartary has no border of its own here. Its outline is the three ruled parts put together and carried to the coast, which is a reading of where the big letters lie.
The line round Independent Tartary also takes in Tibet, though the name is lettered far to the north of it. The sheet does not say whether Tibet was meant to count as Tartary.

Muscovite Tartary is drawn as the whole compartment inside the engraved line, from the White Sea and the Volga to Lake Baikal. The Yakut country and the far north-east are outside that line on this sheet, even though Russia held them.
The dotted line used to part Western from Eastern Tartary is not labelled on the sheet.
North-east Siberia, the Lena, the Amur mouth and Lake Baikal are drawn from hearsay and sit hundreds of kilometres out of place, so the outlines are rough on today's map in that corner.

lands.name: GRANDE TARTARIE
lands.note: The sheet draws no limit for this name. GRANDE TARTARIE is lettered once, in the largest capitals of inner Asia, in one line from the Volga and Yaik (the G stands on the Muscovite side of the border) across the Kalmyk country, the Kirghiz and Lake Baikal to the Amur. It crosses the Muscovite, Independent and Chinese parts, so the ring is taken as all of them together. North and north-east: the Arctic and Pacific coast as drawn, taking in the land of Jelmer, the Yakuts (LES JAKUTI) and the plain of Bargu, which the engraved lines and the colour set apart from Muscovite Tartary; Novaya Zemlya, which the sheet joins to the mainland, is cut off by a judged line. East and south-east: the coast, the border of Korea and the Great Wall of China (the outer line of Chinese Tartary). South: the outer line of Independent Tartary along the Mogol's states, which takes in the kingdoms of Tibet. West: the Persian border, the Caspian shore and the outer line of Muscovite Tartary against Georgia, Little Tartary and European Muscovy. Whether a reader in 1700 would count Tibet, the Volga lands or the far north-east as Great Tartary the sheet does not say.

lands.name: TARTARIE MOSCOVITE
lands.note: The ring is the compartment in which the name is lettered, shut in by an engraved dotted line and washed pink on this copy. North: the Arctic coast from the Mezen to the mouth of the Yenisei. East: the dotted line from the Yenisei mouth south-east, first against the land of Jelmer (green), then against the Yakuts (LES JAKUTI, yellow), then east along the south side of the plain of Bargu to the head of the Amur country. South: the dotted and dashed line against Chinese Tartary (round Nerchinsk and past Selenginsk and Lake Baikal) and against Independent Tartary (north of the Kalmyks, then down the Yaik to the Caspian). South-west: the Caspian shore past Astrakhan, the border of Georgia, the Black Sea shore at Taman and the line north of Azov against Little Tartary. West: the dotted line against MOSCOVIE EUROPEANE from the Don up past Nizhny Novgorod to the White Sea coast near the Mezen. The lettering itself only runs from Viatka to the Lena country; the compartment also holds Permia, Kazan, Astrakhan and Circassia in the west. The Yakut country and the plain of Bargu (noted on the sheet as held by the Muscovites) are outside the line and coloured differently, so they are left out here, though they were Russian ground.

lands.name: TARTARIE INDEPENDANTE
lands.note: The ring is the compartment in which the name is lettered, shut in by an engraved dotted line and washed green on this copy. North: the dotted line against Muscovite Tartary, from the Yaik mouth north-east, then along the Irtysh and south of the Kirghiz to the south end of Lake Baikal. East: the dashed line and yellow outline of Chinese Tartary, round the kingdom of Kalka, down past Camul and round the kingdom of Tanyu. South: the dotted line against China (Yunnan and Sichuan), the states of Asem and Tipra and the Mogol's states as far as Kashmir and Kabul. West: the Persian border past Balkh and Bukhara's desert, then the east shore of the Caspian. The name itself is lettered only across the middle, from the Caspian to the Mongols. The same line and wash also take in Turkestan, the Uzbeks, Kashgar and all the kingdoms of Tibet (Grand Tibet, Rudoc, Barantola with Lassa), which the lettering does not reach.

lands.name: TARTARIE CHINOISE
lands.note: The ring follows the engraved dashed line with a yellow outline on this copy. North: the line against Muscovite Tartary from Lake Baikal past Selenginsk, round the Nerchinsk bulge to Albazin, then north and along the dotted line under the plain of Bargu to the sea. East: the coast from there past the mouth of the Amur to Korea. South: the border of Korea and Leaoton, then the Great Wall of China to its west end, and round the small kingdom of Tanyu. West: the line against Independent Tartary from Tanyu and Camul north round the kingdom of Kalka to Lake Baikal. The name is lettered in one rising line from Tanyu to the Niuche country and crosses the dotted line between the western and eastern parts.

lands.name: TARTARIE OCCIDENTALE
lands.note: The part of Chinese Tartary west of an engraved dotted line that runs from the Argun south past the Dauri to the east end of the Great Wall. North, south and west sides are the outer line of Chinese Tartary (against Muscovite Tartary, the Great Wall, and Independent Tartary). The first word of the name starts outside this ground, on the green of Independent Tartary beside Tibet, and the second word lies inside it north of the Wall; the ring follows the engraved lines. The dotted line on the east is not said on the sheet to divide Western from Eastern Tartary; that is a reading of where the two names lie.

lands.name: TARTARIE OR.LE
lands.note: The part of Chinese Tartary east of the engraved dotted line from the Argun to the east end of the Great Wall: the country of the Niuche or Bogdoi, Yupi and Nulhan, with the Amur. North: the dotted line under the plain of Bargu. East: the coast. South: the border of Korea and Leaoton. West: the dotted line past the Dauri, and the Nerchinsk bulge of Muscovite Tartary. The name is lettered small along the Amur and its first letters stand on the pink of the Muscovite side.

lands.name: PETITE TARTARIE
lands.note: Follows the orange outline colour all the way round: on the north a line from Oczakow east to the Don country below Borissagorod, on the east and south-east the line down to the Sea of Azov, then the north shore of that sea, and the whole coast of the Crimea.

maps.title: Carte de Tartarie, dressée sur les relations de plusieurs voyageurs de differentes nations et sur quelques observations qui ont été faites dans ce païs la, par Guillaume Del'Isle de l'Academie Royale des Sciences. maps.title_plain: Map of Tartary, drawn from the accounts of several travellers of different nations and from some observations made in that country, by Guillaume Delisle of the Royal Academy of Sciences, Paris 1706
maps.says: Delisle uses Tartary as the name for nearly all of northern and central Asia and splits it by who rules it: Muscovite Tartary across the whole of Siberia, Independent Tartary over the Kalmyk and Uzbek country east of the Caspian, and Chinese Tartary from the Mongol lands to the Pacific, with Western and Eastern Tartary lettered inside the Chinese part. Little Tartary sits apart on the steppe north of the Crimea. Within these broad names the sheet letters kingdoms and peoples of its own, such as the Kingdom of Siberia, the Kalmyks and the Mongols, and it names three smaller groups as Tartars: those of Tyumen, of the Kuban and of Dagestan.
doubts: North-east Siberia is drawn from hearsay: the Lena, Yakutsk and the Amur mouth sit six to seven degrees too far south and the coast beyond the Lena is guesswork, so the fit is poor there (errors of 800 to 1100 km). These places are certain in identity and were kept.
Lake Baikal is drawn very small and the Angara towns are crowded against it, so Irkutsk lands about 750 km off.
Novaya Zemlya is joined to the mainland and no Kamchatka is drawn, so there are no sound fitting points on the far northern and north-eastern edges beyond the Yenisei mouth and the Tugur mouth.
The first T of TARTARIE MOSCOVITE, just west of the Urals near Solikamsk, is half hidden by the border colour and reads almost like an I; its position is taken from the spacing of the letters.
The lower left corner is taken up by the title cartouche, so the south-west has no fitting points below Derbent and west of Khiva.
The neat line is read to about 10 pixels from close views of the four corners.

maps.title: Asiae Recentissima Delineatio, Qua Status et Imperia Totius Orientis unacum Orientalibus Indiis exhibentur Authore Io. Bapt. Homanno Norimbergae
maps.title_plain: The newest drawing of Asia, showing the states and empires of the whole East together with the East Indies, by Johann Baptist Homann of Nuremberg
maps.says: The largest name in the north is TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary. Its letters start east of the Caspian Sea, cross the green land and carry on over the pink land of Siberia to the eastern sea. Inside the green land a second, smaller name reads TARTARIA VAGABUNDORUM INDEPENDENS, the independent Tartary of the wandering peoples, with Kalmyks, Black and Yellow Mongolia, Chagatai and the Uzbeks lettered in it. The yellow land north of the Great Wall is called CHINA EXTRA MUROS SIVE TARTARIA CHINENSIS, China outside the walls or Chinese Tartary, and TARTARIA MINOR, Little Tartary, sits north of the Black Sea. The pink north is lettered SIBERIA and MOSCOVITICUM, so the Russian lands and Great Tartary overlap on this sheet; the Arctic sea north of the Lena is MARE TARTARICUM GLACIALE, and a people called CIRCASSI TARTARI stand north of the Caucasus.
doubts: No year is printed on the sheet. The Library of Congress gives only 17--. The date about 1710 rests on three things seen on the sheet: the title names Homann without the words Imperial Geographer (a title he held from 1715) and there is no privilege line; New Britain near New Guinea is lettered as found by Dampier in 1700; and the Caspian Sea still has the old oval shape lying east to west, which Homann redrew after about 1722. Many Siberian and Amur names (Nersinskoi, Albazin, Naun, Karaul) look taken from the Ides and Witsen maps printed around 1704, which is my own knowledge and not something printed on the sheet. So the sheet was made between about 1704 and 1715; 1710 is the middle of that span, not a reading.
The catalogue notes that the Library's two copies differ in the cartouche. Only this copy was looked at.

TARTARIA MAGNA is read as one name: the eight letters of TARTARIA run from the Yaik to just past Lake Baikal, and the five letters of MAGNA carry on in the same size and direction across pink Siberia. The last two letters of TARTARIA and all of MAGNA stand on the pink land, not the green.

No limit is drawn for TARTARIA MAGNA. Its ring is the whole green land plus the part of pink Siberia the letters cross, from Lake Baikal to the eastern sea. The north side of that pink part, halfway to the lettering SIBERIA and MOSCOVITICUM, is my judgment. A reader could as fairly take the name to cover all of Siberia, or only the green land.

The green body colour is taken as the land of TARTARIA VAGABUNDORUM INDEPENDENS. The green also covers the Kingdom of Astrakhan between the Volga and the Yaik, where the name itself does not reach. Hand colour differs from copy to copy.

TARTARIA CHINENSIS is the yellow land outside the Great Wall. Korea has the same yellow and was cut off along the Yalu by judgment. The western lobe of the yellow, lettered KATTAY and TANGUT, is kept in the ring because the phrase CHINA EXTRA MUROS starts there.

A small MAGNA stands in the yellow land near x 4470 to 4650, y 2430 to 2470. It follows MUGALIA FLAVA on the same line and was read as part of that name (Great Yellow Mongolia), not as a Tartary word.

The large word SINARUM (of the Chinese) runs up through the yellow land; the word that goes before it was not found. The first word of the phrase ending MOSCOVITICUM was not read with certainty either.
TARTARIA MINOR has no drawn limit; the ring's north side below UCRANIA is a judgment. The Black Sea is near the edge of the fitted area, so the size of this land and the countries under it are rough.
The italic note Chinensis Tartariae Littora nondum cognita (shores of Chinese Tartary not yet known) along the east coast is marked as a label but is a remark, not a country name.
The text in the upper right cartouche (Benevole Spectator) and the title do not mention Tartary. The note on Terra Yedso does not either.

Places fit this sheet only roughly: half of them land more than about 190 km from where they belong. Siberia is squeezed from north to south (Yakutsk stands north of the Arctic Circle line), Lake Baikal lies east to west, the Yaik mouth is far too far east because of the oval Caspian, Japan is turned so that Honshu lies east to west, and the Ob has no gulf.
Tobolsk: two town signs stand near the name. The one where the Tobol meets the Irtysh was used.
Nerchinsk was left out because its sign was not certain; Lhasa has a name but no town dot and Tashkent is lettered twice, so both were left out.
The earlier worker's letter positions for the long names were checked against the sheet at reading size and kept where they agreed.
uncertain: The sheet has no printed year. About 1710 is a reasoned guess: after 1704, before Homann became Imperial Geographer in 1715.
Great Tartary has no drawn border here. The outline shown is our reading of how far the letters spread.
The green, pink and yellow were painted by hand on this copy, and other copies may be coloured differently.
The mapmaker drew Siberia, the Caspian Sea and Japan badly out of shape, so the outlines land only roughly on the real earth.
Little Tartary has no drawn border and sits at the edge of the fitted area, so its outline is rough.

maps.says: The titles promise all Tartary, great and little, yet on the map itself the word is used sparingly and is spelled Tataria, without the first r. It is lettered large only twice: Little Tartary north of the Black Sea, and a shortened Tataric. laid over Manchuria under China. Everywhere else it appears only in small notes naming single peoples as Tartars, while the land is lettered Siberia, Yakutia, Turkestan and the Kalmyks.
doubts: The Library of Congress scan is dark and small. Readings were made on a sharper copy of the same plate (BnF Gallica btv1b5963132j) matched to this scan to within about a pixel; all positions are in this scan's pixels.

The two copies are different issues: the Gallica copy has a dedication at upper left and the imprint Norib. A. 1739; this sheet has the French title there and an imprint Norimbergae without a year. The map body was read from the Gallica copy, so a change made to the lettering between the issues would not have been seen, though none was noticed where the two were compared.

After a strip by strip search of the whole map body there is no Great, Russian, Muscovite, Asiatic or Independent Tartary lettered across Siberia or the steppe. 'Grande' and 'majoris et Asiaticae' appear only in the titles.
The large Manchurian word is TATARIC, cut short on the sheet, with no second large word. Whether a full stop follows the C could not be seen.
Still partly read: the small Tarta.. by the Volga (its second line is hidden), and the first letter of PORVTI.
The lower letters of TVRKESTAN and the last letter of ELEVTHI were not placed.
The far north-east (Chukchi cape, Kamchatka) and the Tarim towns sit 250 to 430 km off: the sheet itself is wrong there, the places are kept.
Nine fitting places (marked not sure) were placed from medium views, within about 15 pixels.

lands.name: TATARIA MINOR
lands.note: The ring follows the outline colour and the coast. North: the green outline band that leaves the Dniester near Bender and runs south-east to the Dnieper, which is also the edge of Poland's green outline. North-east: the red line of the Russian border from the Dnieper down to the head of the Sea of Azov by Azov town; a note engraved under the map says the limits between Russia and Little Tartary are marked as settled by the peace of 1739. East: the green band along the edge of the red Russian wash, from Azov down to the Caucasus, with CIRCASSIA and the Kuban Tartars inside. South: the green band along the north foot of the mountains lettered CAVCASVS, against the yellow outline of the Turkish side and Georgia, out to the Black Sea shore. West: the Dniester from the Polish corner down to its mouth, green against the yellow of Moldavia. Everywhere else the ring is the shore as the sheet draws it: the Black Sea, the Crimea joined on at the neck of Perekop, and both shores of the Sea of Azov, which is left out of the ring. The same green is used for Poland, so the colour alone does not prove one land; the lettering does, since TATARIA runs from the Dnieper mouth to Perekop and MINOR is carried on into the Kuban. On this small scan the engraved line under the colour could not be made out, so the limit rests on the colour.

lands.name: TATARIC
lands.note: The sheet draws no limit of its own for this word; the ring is a reading of the lettering, carried out to the nearest limits the sheet shows. North and north-west: the drawn Russian border (red line with the green Chinese outline beside it) from the Argun up to the Hinkan range and along it to the sea opposite the Shantar islands. East: the coast, from there past the mouth of the Amur down to the Korean border, with the lower-rank names Ketchen, Yupi and MANTCHEVX inside. South: the red outline of Korea, then the head of the palisade line that fences off LEAOTONG, which is left outside. West and south-west: a line of my own from the palisade head to the bend of the Argun, passing just under the first T and above CORTCHIN, about halfway to the names MONKOVX and KALKAS; the Mongols are lettered as a separate people there, 'long subject to the Sino Tartars'. DAVRIA, SOLON, TVNGVSI and the Tsitsihar and Kirin towns lie inside.

maps.head: Great Tartary as one colour, Siberia inside it
maps.by: Johann Christoph Homann, on a map of his father Johann Baptist Homann
maps.title: Recentissima Asiae Delineatio, Qua Imperia, ejus Regna, et Status, Unacum novissimis Russorum detectionibus circa Mare Caspium et Terram Yedso alias dict[am Kamtzadaliam] per illor: Expedit: et Excursiones, factis sistuntur dirigente Ioh. Christoph. Homanno M.D. cum Gratiosis: Sac. Caes. Majestatis Privilegio. Noribergae.
maps.title_plain: The newest drawing of Asia, showing its empires, kingdoms and states, together with the latest Russian discoveries around the Caspian Sea and the land of Yedso, also called Kamchatka, made on their expeditions and journeys; directed by Doctor Johann Christoph Homann, with imperial privilege, Nuremberg
maps.says: Homann letters TARTARIA MAGNA, Great Tartary, in the largest letters on the mainland, from the Irtysh to the Pacific, and this copy washes one yellow colour over everything from the Urals and the Caspian to Kamchatka, so that Siberia, the Kalmyk country and Bukhara all sit inside it. The word IMPERIUM RUSSORUM, Empire of the Russians, runs from Europe across the Urals into the same ground, and SIBERIA is lettered just above Tartaria Magna, so Tartary here is a region with Russian Siberia inside it and not a state. Beyond the Amur, inside the green of the Chinese empire, stands TARTARIA CHINENSIS, Chinese Tartary, and north of the Black Sea TARTARIA MINOR, Little Tartary. The Arctic off the Lena is called MARE TARTARICUM and the Circassians are named CIRCASSI TARTARI.
doubts: No year is printed anywhere on the sheet: the title cartouche, the Benevole Spectator note and the margins were all read and none carries a date. The date about 1743 is the Library of Congress catalogue's guess, [1743?], for the Schul-atlas this copy comes from.

The plate itself is older than that atlas. The title names Johann Christoph Homann as director, and he ran the firm only from 1724 to 1730; the note to the reader is signed by his father Johann Baptist Homann as imperial geographer, and he died in 1724. The title also speaks of the newest Russian discoveries round the Caspian and in Kamchatka, which reached print in the early 1720s. So the drawing most likely dates from about 1725 to 1730, and 1743 is only when this copy was sold in an atlas.

The land of Tartaria Magna rests on the hand colouring (one yellow wash and outline), which was added copy by copy; the engraving gives the name no border of its own. Another copy could be coloured differently.

The yellow of Tartaria Magna reaches west of the Caspian over Astrakhan, the Circassian steppe and northern Dagestan to the Sea of Azov. That strip was kept inside the ring because the colour and the engraved Europe and Asia line both put it there, though the big lettering stops far to the east.

Tartaria Chinensis has a drawn limit only on the north (the Amur border) and south (the Great Wall); its west side is a judgement. The green colour of the Chinese empire runs much further west, over NAIADA, CATAY and TANGUT.
Tartaria Minor has no drawn or coloured limit at all; its ring is a reading of the lettering.

North-east Asia is drawn from early Russian reports: Yakutsk and the Lena are set far too far east and north, a huge cape (Swetoi nos, Eis Capo) runs into the Arctic, and the head of the Penzhina gulf and Kamchatka are badly placed, so the fit is poor there (errors of 800 to 1000 km). The great cape and the unnamed north-east point were left out of the fit.
Kamchatka is drawn about three times too wide and hangs south-east; the title equates it with the land of Yedso (Jesso), and a COMPAGNIE LAND is drawn east of it.

Novaya Zemlya is stretched far to the east, so its north-east cape lands about 1000 km off; the Amur mouth, Matsumae (drawn as its own small island) and Basra also fit poorly (500 to 700 km). All were looked at again on the sheet and are the mapmaker's placing, so they were kept.
Aden and the Arabian south coast fit badly (about 800 km when left out) because Aden is the only matched place in that corner.
Pingan in Korea was not used: it is lettered as a province and the town mark could not be tied to Pyongyang with certainty.
A great cape or land marked Incognita, coloured red, is drawn off the north-east corner of Asia; it is not part of any Tartary land here.
The big spread lettering through China was read as IMPERIUM SINARUM; the letter between R and M near the Amur could not be made out.
OLGARIA sive KALMUKI is given as lettered; no first letter could be seen before OLGARIA.

The Benevole Spectator note in the upper right corner and the title cartouche in the lower left lie inside the neat line and are cut out as holes. Neither uses the word Tartary. The note says Asia swells with many empires, mostly Mahometan or pagan, and that only in China and a few islands of the Indies does the cross of Christ triumph.

In the title a figure of the cartouche covers the end of one line after alias dict; the words am Kamtzadaliam are supplied from the library catalogue and from the name KAMTZADALIA lettered on the map.
Lake Baikal is drawn small and upright, and its name on the lake could not be read.
The neat line was read to about 10 pixels from close views of two corners.
uncertain: The sheet prints no year. About 1743 is the library's guess for the school atlas this copy was sold in; the map itself was most likely drawn about 1725 to 1730.
The outline of Great Tartary follows the hand colouring of this one copy. The engraved map gives the name no border of its own.
The west side of Chinese Tartary and all of Little Tartary are our reading of where the lettering sits, since the map draws no limit there.
North-east Siberia and Kamchatka were drawn from early Russian reports and sit hundreds of kilometres from their true places, so the map bends badly there.

lands.name: TARTARIA MAGNA
lands.note: The ring follows the one yellow wash, with its yellow outline, that this copy lays over all of Russian and inner Asia, and TARTARIA MAGNA is the largest name inside it. North: the Arctic coast from the Ob gulf to the north-east point. East: the Pacific coast, with the Kamchatka peninsula, which has the same colour. South: the engraved dotted border with the Chinese empire (green) along the Amur, the Argun and the Selenga and then south-west to the Mogul border, the Mogul border (red), the border of Persia (green) to the Caspian, the Caspian east and north shores, and the Caucasus line with Persia and Georgia. West: the Black Sea and Azov coast of Circassia, then the engraved dashed line, coloured green, that divides Europe from Asia from the Don to the Volga, up the Volga and Kama, over the Urals by Verkhoturye and down the Ob to its mouth. The colour is the evidence that Siberia, the Kalmyk country and Bukhara are meant as parts of Great Tartary; the engraving alone gives the name no limit of its own.

lands.name: TARTARIA CHINENSIS
lands.note: North: the engraved dotted border with the Russian side along the Amur, where the colour changes from green to yellow (firm). East: the coast from the Amur mouth to the Korean border. South: the border of Korea and the Great Wall, drawn as a wall and coloured green. West: no limit is drawn; the ring is closed by judgement about halfway between this name and NAIADA, keeping ALBI KALMAKI, NIKANSKOI and LEAOTUNG inside. The same green wash runs on west over NAIADA, CATAY and TANGUT as far as the Selenga, so the colour would give a larger land than the lettering does.

lands.name: TARTARIA MINOR
lands.note: No limit is drawn and Europe is left uncoloured on this copy apart from a green coast line. South: the Black Sea and Azov coast, with the Crimea, which is lettered in a lower rank. East: the mouth of the Don at Azov. North: about halfway to UCRANIA and the Don country. West: the coast near the Dniester mouth, just beyond the first letters.

maps.head: A Chinese-Tartar kingdom, and peoples called Tatars
maps.by: Johann Matthias Hase, finished by August Gottlob Boehme, published by the Homann Heirs, Nuremberg
maps.title: ASIA secundum legitimas Projectionis Stereographicae regulas et juxta recentissimas observation. et relationes, explosis aliorum fabulosis designationibus et narrationibus, adhibitis quoque veterum monumentis et recentiorum itinerariis descripta, et in partes suas methodicas IX divisa a I. Matth. Hasio M.P.P.O. nunc ex beate defuncti subsidiis et M.S.C.tis designata a M. August. Gottlob Boehmio. Impensis Homannianorum Hered. A. 1744
maps.title_plain: Asia, drawn by the true rules of stereographic projection and from the newest observations and reports, with other people's fabled drawings and tales thrown out, using old records and recent travellers' routes, and divided into its nine orderly parts by J. Matthias Hase; now drawn from the late author's materials and manuscripts by August Gottlob Boehme, at the cost of the Homann Heirs, 1744
maps.says: This sheet has no country called Tartary at all, and it spells the word Tatar, without the first r. The only big name that holds the word is REGNVM SINO TATARIC, the Chinese-Tartar Kingdom, spread from the south of China to the Amur: of the nine parts the title promises, this is the only one with a Tartar name, and it means the empire of China under its Manchu rulers. Everywhere else the word is a name for peoples: Crimean, Kuban, Nogai, Ufa and Bashkir Tatars inside or beside Russia, Khivan and Burut Tatars in the middle, Kokonor and Ordos Tatars by China. The north is SIBERIA and IAKVTIA inside the Russian empire, and inner Asia is shared out among Kalmyks, Eleuths, Bukharia, Turkestan, Mongols and Tibet.
doubts: The date 1744 is printed in the title cartouche ('Impensis Homannianorum Hered. A. 1744'). Hase died in 1742; the cartouche says Boehme drew the map from his materials.

The title says Asia is divided into nine parts, but the sheet has no list or key of the nine parts; they are shown only by outline colours. Which nine Hase meant was not read off the sheet. Only one of the big coloured parts carries a Tartar name.

REGNVM SINO TATARIC: the letters were read one by one across China and Manchuria. No letters were found after the C near the Amur, so the word seems cut short (for Tataricum). The first word REGNVM lies in Yunnan and Suchuen.

The land of REGNVM SINO TATARIC is traced as the whole green-outlined empire, China proper included, because the name runs across both. A visitor comparing with other maps should know that 'Chinese Tartary' on other sheets means only the part north of the Great Wall.
The sheet joins a land called Terra Yeso to the mainland south of the Amur mouth and colours it green; it is inside the ring. This coast is drawn by guess.
Korea's northern limit in the ring is judged; the border there is weak on this copy.
CHIWINSKI TAT (east of the Aral Sea): the first eight letters are clear; the last letters are small, damaged and partly hidden by a river, and the reading TAT is not certain.
TA[T]I CRIMÆÆ: spread capitals from the Kerch Strait over the Kuban; one letter is hidden by the coast shading. Taken as Crimean Tatars.
VFFIMI Tatari: the first letter was not clear.
The small notes 'Tatari' with BASKIRI and 'Tat' with BRVTTI are in small letters beside spread capitals.
A long French title is printed in the top margin, outside the map border; it was not read in full and is not marked as a label. No Tartary word was noticed in it or in the Latin title.

No bare TATARIA, TATARIA MAGNA, Russian, Independent or Little Tartary was found anywhere on the sheet after a full search in strips. Small names under the stains near Kokonor and along the folds could hide a word.
Lhasa fits badly (about 680 km): Hase puts it too far south-east. Aden and the strait of Bab el Mandeb, the Malay tip and the Lena mouth also fit loosely; they are at the edges of the sheet.
Kandahar was left out of the fit because it was not certain which town sign belongs to the name.
The north-east (Chukchi land, Kamchatka's north) is drawn from hearsay; a note on the sheet says the coast is known only from the reports of the people living there.
Pixels for Beijing, Xi'an and Albazin were worked back from a rotated picture and may be off by ten to twenty pixels.
The Aral Sea is drawn much too small and too far south; its middle is matched to the middle of the real sea.
uncertain: There is no land called Tartary on this sheet. The outline shown is the whole Chinese empire, which the map calls the Chinese-Tartar Kingdom.
The big name seems cut short on the sheet: it ends TATARIC near the Amur.
The map joins a guessed land called Yeso to the mainland coast; it is inside the outline.
Two of the Tatar people names (by the Aral Sea and by the Crimea) are hard to read and may be read wrongly.
The title speaks of nine parts of Asia but the sheet does not list them.

lands.name: REGNVM SINO TATARIC
lands.note: The name is spread from Yunnan to the Amur, so it covers China proper and the Manchu and Mongol lands together. North and west: the dotted border with the Russian empire and the Kalmyk lands, washed orange on the outer side and green on the inner side, from the Altai past Lake Baikal's south, up the Argun and along the mountains to the sea near Udskoy. East: the coast as drawn, including the land lettered Terra Yeso that the sheet joins to the mainland south of the Amur and colours green; Sakhalin and Korea are left out (Korea has its own outline and its own name as a kingdom; its northern limit is judged, the sheet draws it weakly). South-east and south: the China coast and the dotted, colour-washed border with Tonkin and Ava. West: the blue-green outline of China proper up to Sining, then the dotted green and yellow border north of Kokonor round to Hami and Turfan. Kokonor and Tibet lie outside the outline. A blue-green line inside the ring (along the Great Wall) sets China proper apart from the northern lands, but the name runs across it.
