maps.head: Three Tartaries, named by who rules
maps.by: Jean Palairet, with additions by Louis Delarochette; printed in London for John Bowles and Carington Bowles
maps.title: A MAP of ASIA with its Principal DIVISIONS by J. Palaret, with several Additions & Improvements by L. Delarochette.
maps.title_plain: A map of Asia with its main divisions, by J. Palairet, with additions and improvements by L. Delarochette
maps.says: This sheet letters RUSSIAN TARTARY by the lower Volga, INDEPENDENT TARTARY across inner Asia from the Caspian to Tibet, and CHINESE TARTARY in one long curve from the Great Wall to the Amur, with LITTLE TARTARY north of the Black Sea. A table printed on the map spells the scheme out: Russian Tartary is the kingdoms of Kasan and Astrachan and part of Circassia; Independent Tartary is the Kara Kalpaks, Turkestan, the Usbecs and the Kingdom of the Eluts with both Bukarias and both Tibets; Chinese Tartary is the Western and Eastern Monguls and the Tartars of Kokonor. Everything north of these is RUSSIA IN ASIA and SIBERIA, with its provinces named, and the word Tartary is not used there at all. There is no Great Tartary on this sheet: the name only appears with a ruler's or a people's name in front of it.
doubts: The table 'Methodical Divisions of Asia' at lower left reads, for the continent: '1st RUSSIA in ASIA: Russian Tartary which Compreh.ds Kingdom of Kasan, Governm.t of Astrachan, Part of Circassia where is Terki; Siberia: Tobolskoi, Jenisseiskoi, Jakuckoi, Ochockoi which includes the Peninsula of Kamczatki.' '2d INDEP.T TARTARY: The Kara or Black Kalpack; Turkestan; Usbec: Great Bukaria, the Antient Bactriana where is Balk, Dagistan; K.m of the Eluts which is a remainder of the Empire of Zingis Kan: Kalmakia, Little Bukaria, Little Tibet, Gr. Tibet (the State of the Dalai Lama).' '3d CHINESE TARTARY: Western Monguls, Eastern Monguls, Tartars of Kokonor, Divided into several Principalities, Hords & Tribes of Tartars.'
The imprint under the table reads 'London, Printed for John Bowles at the Black Horse in Cornhil, and Carington Bowles next the Chapter House in St. Pauls Church Yard.' No year is printed there.
The title cartouche reads 'A MAP of ASIA with its Principal DIVISIONS by J. Palaret, with several Additions & Improvements by L. Delarochette.' The name is spelt Palaret on the sheet.

No year is printed anywhere on the sheet that I could find. The Library of Congress gives '17--?'. 1755 is the year of Palairet's atlas, for which the map was first made; the sheet itself is a later state 'with several Additions & Improvements by L. Delarochette' printed for John Bowles and Carington Bowles. As far as I know Carington Bowles traded at St Paul's Church Yard from about 1764, so this printing is likely some years after 1755; I have not checked that against a reference.

The latest dates lettered on the map itself are 'Beerings I. where he was cast away and Died 1741', a 'Land seen ... in 1741', and a note that Anson took the Acapulco ship on '1 July 174-' where the last figure reads as 3 or 7. So the drawing cannot be older than the 1740s.

Under RUSSIAN TARTARY, east of the Volga, a smaller name reads 'R.ME D'ASTRACAN', which looks like French (Royaume d'Astracan) left on an English plate; the first letters are small and I am not sure of them.

CHINESE TARTARY is one long curve of letters; EASTERN and MONGALS are lettered beside its second half and WESTERN MONGALS to the west. I read EASTERN as going with MONGALS (the table lists 'Eastern Monguls'), not with TARTARY.

Hand colour and engraving disagree for Chinese Tartary: the red outline of China runs outside the Great Wall, and the outer Mongols share the yellow of Russia. The land was traced from the engraved dotted lines, the Wall, the lettering and the table.
Little Tartary has no drawn limit; its ring is a narrow guess round the lettering and the Crimea.
Udskoi, the Anadyr, the Chukchi cape and Herat fit badly because the sheet misplaces them; Orenburg was left out of the fit because I am not sure which site is meant.
The southern third of the sheet (India, Indochina, the islands) and the Pacific margin were searched for the word Tartary at a smaller size than the north; I found none there.
uncertain: No year is printed on the sheet. 'About 1755' comes from the date of Palairet's atlas; this copy was printed for the Bowles family and may be ten years or so later.
The engraving and the hand colour disagree about Chinese Tartary. The outline here follows the engraved lines, the Great Wall and the table, not the colour.
Little Tartary has no drawn limit; its outline is only a reading of where the letters sit.
Russian Tartary is drawn from the table's list (Kasan, Astrachan, part of Circassia); the name itself is lettered only near Astrakhan.
The far north-east of Asia, the land by the Sea of Okhotsk and the east of Persia are badly placed on the sheet, so the bend is rough there.

lands.name: LITTLE TARTARY
lands.note: The sheet draws no limit for this name; it lies in the Europe margin, which is one flat colour. South: the Black Sea coast, the Crimea and the north shore of the Sea of Asof as drawn. East: stopped at Asof, where the lettering ends. North and west: only my reading, a narrow band just past the lettering.

lands.name: RUSSIAN TARTARY
lands.note: The table on the sheet says Russian Tartary takes in the Kingdom of Kasan, the Government of Astrachan and the part of Circassia where Terki is, and the ring joins those three as engraved. West and north: the dashed line that parts Europe from Asia, from the Don country up round Cazan. East: the dotted line down the Urals and round Orenburg to the river Jaick. South: the Caspian shore to Terki, then the engraved and red-coloured limit of Circassia back to the Black Sea. The colourist gave Circassia a red outline and Kasan and Astracan a yellow one, so the colour splits what the table and the lettering join; the south limit of Circassia was read at small size. The province lettered Ufimskoi, with Ufa and Orenburg, lies west of the Urals inside the same outer line and is taken in with Kasan, though the table does not name it.

lands.name: INDEPENDENT TARTARY
lands.note: An engraved dotted line with a yellow outline wash runs nearly all the way round. North: the dotted Russian frontier from the river Jaick past Orenburg, along the desert of Ischimska to the Irtis, up the Irtis and round Lake Saissan. East: the dotted line down from the Asajanskoi country to the red line of China, then that red line round Hami and Turfan, down past Kokonor to the edge of Yunnan. South: the limit against Asam and Ava and the red line of the Mogul's India. West: the limit of Persia from the Indus country up past Kandahar and Bokara to the Caspian, then the east shore of the Caspian. This is the ground the table gives to 'Indep.t Tartary': the Kara Kalpaks, Turkestan, the Usbecs and the Kingdom of the Eluts with both Bukarias and both Tibets. The stretch between the Irtis and Lake Saissan and the south-east corner by Yunnan were read at small size.

lands.name: CHINESE TARTARY
lands.note: Traced from the engraved lines, the lettering and the table, not from the colour. North: the dotted Russian frontier from the Selinga country to the river Argun, then the dotted line north of the Amur to the sea opposite Sangalien island. East: the coast down to Korea. South: the engraved limit of Korea, the shore of Leaotong, then the Great Wall from the Gulf of Pekeli west, south of the Ortos country, out to its west end beyond Kantcheou, and back along the faint pink limit that parts the Tartars of Kokonor from Shensi. West: the red line against the Kingdom of the Eluts round Hami and Turfan and the dotted line up to the Russian frontier. The table names its parts as the Western Monguls, the Eastern Monguls and the Tartars of Kokonor. The colourist did otherwise: the red outline of China runs outside the Wall and takes in the Mongous, Leaotong, Hami and Kokonor, while the Western and Eastern Mongals are left in the same yellow as Russia and Independent Tartary. Leaotong, behind its fence of stakes, is included here because it lies outside the Wall; that is my judgment. The limit of Kokonor on the Chinese side is a faint pink line read at small size.

maps.head: Three Tartarys, cut apart like a puzzle
maps.by: No mapmaker is named on the sheet. Sold in London by T. Woodman and H. Mutlow, successors to Spilsbury's shop
maps.title: ASIA, Divided Into Its Empires, Kingdoms and States, with their General Subdivisions. LONDON: Sold by T. Woodman & H. Mutlow, (late Spilsbury's) No. 30, Russel Court, Covent Garden. 1772.
maps.title_plain: Asia, divided into its empires, kingdoms and states, with their general subdivisions. London: sold by T. Woodman and H. Mutlow (formerly Spilsbury's shop), 30 Russell Court, Covent Garden, 1772
maps.says: This sheet letters the word four times as a country. RUSSIAN TARTARY runs across the yellow Russian country from Tobolsk to the Okhotsk coast, under the name SIBERIA, which is lettered over the same ground further north. CHINESE TARTARY runs across the brown country of the Western and Eastern Mongals, from the Great Wall to the Amur. The bare word TARTARY, in the largest letters, is kept for the uncoloured country between them, from the Caspian to the edge of China, where the sheet also letters KASACCIA HORDA, USBECKS, KHARASM, TURKISTAN, GREAT BUKARIA, LITTLE BUKARIA, KALMUKS and ELUTS. LITTLE TARTARY is a small name north of the Black Sea, and two small notes name peoples: the Tartars of Kokonor and the Mantcheu Tartars who subdued China.
doubts: The date 1772 is printed on the title piece, so it is read from the sheet. The seller's line (Sold by T. Woodman & H. Mutlow, late Spilsbury's) is on a paper slip pasted over an older imprint, as the library's note also says, so this copy was put on sale later than 1772 by the shop that took over from Spilsbury. The year is the date of the plate, not of this pasted label.
No mapmaker or engraver is named anywhere I could read on the sheet. The drawing of Asia looks like the French maps of d'Anville put into English, but the sheet does not say so.

This copy is a dissected map: it was pasted on wood and cut into puzzle pieces along the borders. The dark wavy lines are saw cuts, with knobs and gaps here and there, and a few letters are lost in the cuts. The rings follow the borders and not the knobs.

The fit of the matched places was left as the earlier worker made it, with three marks moved after looking again: Atyrau (to the Jaik mouth below the name Gurjew), the head of Penzhina bay, and Cape Dezhnev.

The north-east corner fits worst (Cape Dezhnev, Penzhina bay, Udskoye, Svyatoy Nos, Nova Zemla): the sheet draws the Tchuktschi land and Kamtschatka too small and the Okhotsk coast too far east, and the land runs past the top border line. These are the mapmaker's errors and are kept.
Mogadishu and Brunei fit badly, but both lie in the far corners of the sheet, outside the dial frame.

RUSSIAN TARTARY and SIBERIA are both lettered across the same yellow country and the sheet draws no line between them. The ring for RUSSIAN TARTARY is the whole yellow wash of Russia in Asia. The lettering itself only runs from near Tobolsk to the Okhotsk country, so the Astracan and Ufa corner west of the Urals' south end and the far north-east are inside the ring by colour only.

The west side of the RUSSIAN TARTARY ring between Czariczin and Astracan follows the lower Volga, where the wash changes from the yellow of the Kingdom of Astracan to the paler Circassia. The change of colour there is faint and I judged it.

The bare word TARTARY has no word like Independent before it. I looked along the whole run of the letters and to the west of the first T. Its last letter Y stands south of the border line, on the north edge of the Tibet piece; the ring keeps to the line.

The large TARTARY could also be meant as a general name for the whole of inner Asia, with Russian and Chinese Tartary as its parts. The sheet does not say. Because the letters stay inside the uncoloured country, it is recorded as a land of its own and not as the whole.

The Tangut and Kokonor country is a separate puzzle piece with a dotted line round it. It has the same brown wash as Chinese Tartary, so it is inside the CHINESE TARTARY ring, but the lettering CHINESE TARTARY starts just east of it. A reader could also take it as a land of its own.
Leaotong, inside the Intrenchment of Stakes, has the pale colour of China and is left out of Chinese Tartary. Corea has its own colour and is left out.

LITTLE TARTARY has no drawn limit. Its ring is a modest band round the lettering down to the coast. Europe is almost empty on this sheet and few matched places hold that corner, so on the earth the ring slides west over Moldova and Romania more than the mapmaker would have meant. The Crimea is named but has no coast of its own here.
In the first A of the second word of CHINESE TARTARY the letter is half hidden by town names; its place on the spine is judged from its neighbours.
SIBERIA: the letters S, I, B, E, R, I were found; the last A, somewhere near the Kolyma, was not found for sure, so the spine stops at the second I.
USBECKS: the letters U S B E C K were found; a final S was not seen for sure. TANGUT: only T A N G are clear before a saw cut.
The note 'Ancient Land of the Mantcheu Tartars who subdued China' is three lines of small script. It is marked as one people label on its middle line.
The sea and island half of the sheet (India, the East Indies, the Pacific) was looked over at small size only; no Tartary lettering was seen there.
Longitude on this sheet is counted east from Ferro (lettered in the bottom margin), which is why the numbers along the border are about 18 degrees higher than today's.
uncertain: The year 1772 is printed on the title, but the seller's name is on a slip pasted over an older one, so this copy was sold some years later.
No mapmaker is named on the sheet.
Russian Tartary and Siberia are lettered over the same yellow country with no line between them, so the outline for Russian Tartary is the whole of Russia in Asia as coloured.
The big bare word Tartary may be meant for the middle country only, as shown here, or as a general name for all of inner Asia. The sheet does not say.
Tangut and Kokonor are coloured like Chinese Tartary and are drawn inside it here, but they are a separate piece with their own dotted line.
Little Tartary has no border on this sheet, and the far north-east of Asia is drawn badly, so both sit loosely on the real earth.

lands.name: RUSSIAN TARTARY
lands.note: The ring is the yellow wash of the Russian country in Asia, which on this dissected copy is also where the wooden pieces were cut. North and east: the coast as drawn, from Waygatz to Kamtschatka and round to the Uda River (the Ob gulf is crossed at its mouth; islands are left out). South: the cut and colour line against Chinese Tartary from the Uda to the Altai, then against the uncoloured Tartary to the north shore of the Caspian. West: the lower Volga from Astracan up to Czariczin, then the inner edge of the orange band that marks the limit of Europe, up the Poyas or Belt mountains (the Urals) to Waygatz. The sheet letters both SIBERIA and RUSSIAN TARTARY over this same ground and draws no line between them; the lettering RUSSIAN TARTARY itself only runs from near Tobolsk to the Okhotsk country, so the Astracan and Ufa corner and the far north-east are in the ring by colour, not by lettering.

lands.name: TARTARY
lands.note: The ring is the ground left without a body wash between the yellow Russian country, the brown Chinese Tartary, and the washes of Persia, India and Tibet; the puzzle pieces are cut on the same lines, and a dotted engraved line runs along parts of them. North: the line against the Russian country from the Caspian by the Jemba to the Altai. East: the line against Chinese Tartary, down the west side of the Western Mongals and round the west side of Tangut. South: the lines against Tibet, India (Cabul, Kashmir) and Persia (Korasan). West: the east shore of the Caspian. The last letter Y of TARTARY stands just south of the south line, on the north edge of the Tibet piece; the ring follows the line, not the letter.

lands.name: CHINESE TARTARY
lands.note: The ring is the brown wash, cut as puzzle pieces along the same lines. North: the line against the Russian country from the Altai past Selinginsk and the Argun to the Uda River mouth. East: the coast from the Uda past the Amur mouth to the Corean Sea (the island of Sahalien-Ula Hata is left out). South: the line against Corea, the Intrenchment of Stakes round Leaotong (left outside), and the Great Wall. West: the line against the uncoloured Tartary. The Tangut and Kokonor country in the south-west is a separate puzzle piece with a dotted line round it but carries the same brown wash, so it is taken into the ring; the lettering CHINESE TARTARY does not reach it.

lands.name: LITTLE TARTARY
lands.note: The sheet draws no limit: the name is lettered in the bare Europe corner. South: the coast of the Black Sea and the Sea of Asof as drawn (the orange Europe edge), from west of Precop to Asof. North, east and west: a modest band round the lettering, kept short of the large letters of EUROPE. The Crimea is named (Krim, Caffa, Baczisarai) but drawn without a coast of its own, so it is left out.

maps.head: Three Tartaries, and Siberia is not one
maps.title: Bowles's New One-Sheet Map of Asia, divided into its Empires, Kingdoms, States, and other Subdivisions; laid down from Observations of the most Celebrated Geographers. London: Printed for the Proprietor Carington Bowles, No. 69 St. Paul's Church Yard.
maps.title_plain: Bowles's new one-sheet map of Asia, divided into its empires, kingdoms, states and other subdivisions, drawn from the observations of the best known geographers. Printed in London for Carington Bowles.
maps.says: Bowles letters three large Tartaries and gives each a drawn border. Russian Tartary is only the pink country between the Black Sea, the Volga and the Urals; Independent Tartary is the green-edged country from the Caspian to Hami; Chinese Tartary is the ground north of the Great Wall from Mongolia to the Pacific, inside the pink wash of the Chinese empire. The whole north is lettered RUSSIAN EMPIRE and SIBERIA, with no Tartary in its name, and Little Tartary is a small name north of the Crimea. Inside the Tartaries the sheet names peoples of its own, such as the Kalmucks, Eluths, Usbecks, Kalkas, Mongols and Manchew Tartars. A table in the corner lists Tartary as one division of Asia made of Chinese, Independent, 'Tibet or Mogulean' and Russian Tartary, and lists 'Russ. Tartary' again under Russia in Asia beside Siberia.
doubts: The date 1791 is printed below the bottom border: 'Published as the Act directs, 4 June 1791'. Inside the title oval someone has written 1784 by hand in pencil or ink; that is not printed and was not used.
The corner table calls Tibet 'Tibet or Mogulean Tartary', but on the map itself Tibet is lettered TIBET OR BOOTAN and GREAT TIBET with no Tartary, so no label or land was made for it.

The table and the title oval are text blocks, not map lettering, so the Tartary names in the table are not marked as labels. The table, the title oval, the scale box and the compass rose are cut out as holes.

Chinese Tartary shares one pink wash with China, Korea and the Koko Nor country. Its south side is taken as the Great Wall and the red line round Leaotong. West of the end of the Wall near Sochew the sheet draws no line, so the ring is cut straight across to the western border; that stretch is my judgement.

Whether the Tartars of Koko Nor and the Hami and Sha-tcheu corner were meant as part of Chinese Tartary is not shown by any line. The Hami corner is inside the ring because it lies north of the Wall's end; Koko Nor is outside.
Sagaleen island is outlined in the same red as the Chinese coast but is left out of the Chinese Tartary ring, which is a single outline.

Russian Tartary is lettered only over the Volga and Ural country, but the pink wash and red outline also take in Astracan, Cuban and Circassia down to the Caucasus. The ring follows the wash and outline.
Little Tartary has no border and no colour. Its ring is my reading of the lettering between the Dnieper mouth and the Don, and the Crimea is left outside.
At the Balk corner the green Persian border makes a deep bend south of the Amu; I read Balk, Talkan and Bamien as lying on the Independent Tartary side of it.
Independent Tartary and Persia have much the same pale green wash; the engraved dashed line with its darker green edge is what parts them.
A river on the Manchurian coast near 5740,2480 reads 'Tartan R.' or 'Tarfan R.'; the third letter is unclear and it was not marked.
'Tartura' on the coast of Palestine is the town of Tantura and has nothing to do with Tartary; it was not marked.
The Arctic coast east of the Yenisei is drawn from rough Russian reports: the Olenek mouth, Svyatoy Nos and East Cape fit 240 to 300 km off. They are certain in identity and were kept.
The points for the Ob mouth, the Yugorsky Strait, the Khatanga mouth and Turukhansk (lettered Mangazeja and Turugansk side by side) were placed on small features and may be 10 to 20 pixels off.

Ochakov, Suez, Tokyo, Aden and Mocha fit 240 to 330 km off; Ochakov, Aden and Mocha were checked on close views and are taken as the mapmaker's own errors. They lie outside or at the edge of the dial frame.
The far south and east of the sheet (Arabia, India, the East Indies, the Pacific) were read once at reading size for Tartary lettering and none was seen; they were not read a second time.
Label positions for RUSSIAN EMPIRE, SIBERIA and CHINA were read from the reduced strips and are good to about 15 pixels.
The neat line is read to about 5 pixels from close views of three corners; the sheet is very slightly skewed.
uncertain: Chinese Tartary has the same pink colour as China. Its south side is taken as the Great Wall, and one short stretch in the west, past the end of the Wall, has no drawn line at all.
Russian Tartary is lettered only over the Volga and Ural country, but the pink colour it sits in runs down to the Caucasus. The outline follows the colour.
Little Tartary has no border on this sheet. Its outline is a reading of where the name is lettered, north of the Crimea.
The corner table also speaks of 'Tibet or Mogulean Tartary', but the map itself never letters Tartary on Tibet.
The far north-east coast of Siberia is drawn roughly, so the fit is 200 to 300 km off there.
The date 1791 is printed under the bottom border. A handwritten 1784 inside the title oval is not part of the print.

West: the dashed line where the pink meets the green of Independent Tartary. The whole of this ground shares one pink wash with China itself, so the wash does not set Chinese Tartary apart; the Wall does. The Kalkas, the Mongols and the Manchew Tartars are lettered inside it in smaller letters. Sagaleen island, outlined in the same red, is left out of the ring.

South: the dashed line shared with Independent Tartary down to the Yemba mouth, the north shore of the Caspian, then the dashed line along the Caucasus to the Black Sea. West: the Black Sea shore, the strait of Kerch and the Sea of Azov. East: the Don, where the pink Russian wash begins. North and west: a line a little above the lettering, about halfway to the lettering RUSSIA IN EUROPE, closed at the Dnieper mouth. The Crimea, lettered separately, is left outside.

maps.title: MODERN ASIA.
maps.title_plain: Modern Asia
maps.says: This small sheet writes Tartary only twice. Western Tartary is the pink country between the Caspian and the Gobi, holding Turkestan, Bucharia, the Dzungars and Kashgar, with Tibet coloured as part of the same block. Chinese Tartary is the green country of the Mongols and Manchus north of China, while everything Russian is called Siberia and split into Tobolsk, Yakutsk and other governments with no Tartary name at all.
doubts: The scan is small (2601 by 3271), so town rings can only be placed to about 5 pixels, which is 40 km or so on the ground.

Only two Tartary names are on the sheet, each set on two lines: WESTERN over TARTARY, and CHINESE (north of the Amur) with TARTARY far to the south of it. No Russian, Independent or Eastern Tartary is lettered.
Tibet and Little Tibet share the pink colour of Western Tartary, so the colour block is wider than the name strictly says.
Arabia and the Red Sea fit worst (Mecca and Bab el Mandeb are 500 to 600 km off when left out): the sheet draws the Red Sea too far west and sets Mecca deep inland.
The Arctic coast from Novaya Zemlya to the Lena is loosely drawn; the Gulf of Ob, Taimyr and Lena mouth spots are approximate.
Okhotsk has no town symbol and the head of Penzhina Bay is unnamed; both are read from the coast shape.
The also list is capped at eight; Bucharia, Calmucs, Great Turky, Buratians, Tungusi and the Russian governments of Astrachan, Orenburg and Irkutsk are also lettered in this country.
The spines for the YAKUTSK and TOBOLSK government names are approximate, as their letters are widely spread among other lettering.
Both Tartary lands have an engraved dotted border with the colour laid on it; the rings were placed to about 5 pixels on a small scan, so they may sit 40 km or so off the line in places.
Western Tartary is traced to the dotted line with a thin red edge that runs inside the pink from Cabul to the Coby, so Thibet and Little Thibet, though washed the same pink, are left out of it.
The Sea of Aral is left out of the Western Tartary ring as a notch from the north, since its northern end touches the Russian border; the shore there is small and blurred.

The green of Chinese Tartary runs south-west over the Coby or Shamo desert and the Calmucs country to the corner of China and Thibet; the ring follows the green and the dotted line, although the lettering CHINESE TARTARY itself sits only over the Amur, Mongol and Manchu country.
Leaotong is washed yellow with China and cut off from the green by a dotted line, so it is left out of Chinese Tartary.
The islands of Sagaleen and Jesso are edged green like Chinese Tartary, but they are islands with names of their own and are not counted in its ring.
The small Russian wedge between the Onon and the Argun, where the border steps north to the Amur, is blurred; the ring there is good to perhaps 10 pixels.
A second look over the whole sheet found no other Tartar lettering: the Black Sea side has Taurica and Nogaye, not Little Tartary or Crim Tartary.

maps.by: Robert Laurie and James Whittle, London
maps.title: ASIA with ITS ISLANDS, and DIFFERENT REGIONS according to THEIR MODERN DIVISIONS; also THE DISCOVERIES made by CAPT. COOK. LONDON. Published 12th. May 1799, by LAURIE & WHITTLE, No. 53, Fleet Street.
maps.title_plain: Asia with its islands and different regions, according to their modern divisions, with the discoveries made by Captain Cook
maps.says: This London sheet still letters the word across most of inner and north Asia. RUSSIAN TARTARY runs along the south of Russian Asia under SIBERIA, in letters of the same size and with no line between the two. TARTARY alone, in the largest letters, crosses a pink country with a dotted border from the Caspian to the Gobi, and inside it stand the Kasaccia Horda, Usbeck, Kharasm, Turkistan, Great and Little Bukaria, the Kalmuks and the Eluts. CHINESE TARTARY, marked off by the same kind of border and split by the words WESTERN and EASTERN, runs on to the Pacific north of the Great Wall, with the Mongals lettered in both halves; LITTLE TARTARY sits north of the Black Sea and the strait beside Saghalien is the CHANNEL OF TARTARY.
doubts: The date is printed in the title cartouche: Published 12th May 1799. No mapmaker or engraver is named on the sheet, only the publishers Laurie and Whittle. A pencil note in the bottom margin and the library catalogue say this copy comes from their Imperial Sheet Atlas of 1803.
The title cartouche (top left, over northern Europe) and the oval of scale bars (bottom left, over the Indian Ocean) are cut out as holes. The longitude scale counts from Ferro Island.

Labels checked letter by letter: the big slanting word in the pink country is TARTARY alone. There is no INDEPENDENT on the sheet. WESTERN and EASTERN each stand alone, with no TARTARY of their own, beside the two halves of the big CHINESE TARTARY lettering, so I read them as Western and Eastern Chinese Tartary.

The word Tartar also appears in TARTARS OF KOKONOR (two lines), in the small note 'Antient Land of the Mantcheu Tartars who subdued China' north of Corea, and in CHANNEL OF TARTARY. I found no other Tartar lettering; the title does not use the word.

RUSSIAN TARTARY has no limit of its own. Its north side is my line halfway between its letters and the letters of SIBERIA, and its west side is my line just west of its first letter. Only its south side (the Russian border) and its coast are drawn on the sheet. Its size depends almost wholly on where I put the north line.

TARTARY: the pink body colour runs from the Caspian over Tibet as well, as one wash, and the last letter Y of TARTARY stands inside Tibet. I cut Tibet off along a dotted line that runs from Cashmir to the Gobi and that I read as the north limit of Tibet; it could also be a caravan road. TIBET or STATE OF THE DALAI LAMA has its own large name, so I left it out. With Tibet counted in, this Tartary would be a good deal larger; I did not measure by how much.
The Aral is drawn as a long thin lake leaning north-east and is outlined in red like a border; it lies inside Tartary.

CHINESE TARTARY: the limit is a dotted line with green outline colour nearly all round. Ortos (inside the bend of the Yellow River), Tangut and Kokonor are inside it; Leaotong is outlined yellow with China and left out; Corea has its own colour. Saghalien and the land of Jesso are outlined green as well but are not in the ring.
The line between WESTERN and EASTERN is my own, along a chain of hills from Lake Kulon to the Great Wall. The sheet draws no boundary between them and letters MONGALS on both sides.

LITTLE TARTARY: Europe is uncoloured and has no border lines here, so the ring is a modest reading of the lettering on the mainland north of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The Crimea (lettered Krim) is left out; a reader of the time might well have counted it in. The Black Sea is drawn squeezed at the edge of the sheet and there are few matched places west of the Crimea, so on the real earth this land falls partly on Moldova and Romania.
Constantinople has no clear town mark and is kept out of the fit. I added the neck of Precop as a matched place; it fits to about 130 km.

Places that fit badly and were kept as the mapmaker's errors: Orenburg (about 480 km; drawn at the head of the Jaik far east of the present town), the mouth of the Lena (about 450 km; the Arctic coast east of the Taymyr is drawn too far south and west), East Cape (about 430 km), Aden (about 410 km), the mouth of the Yenisei, Tashkent and Bukhara (each about 330 km).
In TANGUT the fifth letter is hard to read under the border colour. A third Mongol name, lettered MONGOUS north of the Great Wall, was not recorded in the other names.
uncertain: Russian Tartary and Siberia are two names in the same country with no line drawn between them. Where one stops and the other starts is our own halfway line.
The pink colour of Tartary runs on over Tibet. We cut Tibet off along a dotted line on the sheet because Tibet has its own big name, but the last letter of TARTARY does stand inside Tibet.
Western and Eastern are single words in the two halves of Chinese Tartary. The line between them is ours, along a chain of hills; the sheet draws none.
Little Tartary has no border or colour on this sheet. Its outline is only our reading of where the name is written, and it leaves out the Crimea.
The mapmaker put some places a few hundred kilometres out (Orenburg, the Arctic river mouths, the far north-east), so the bent sheet is off by that much in those parts.

lands.name: RUSSIAN TARTARY
lands.note: The sheet draws no line between RUSSIAN TARTARY and SIBERIA: the two names are spread in letters of the same size across Russian Asia, SIBERIA above and RUSSIAN TARTARY below. North: my own line, halfway between the two rows of letters. East: the shore of the Sea of Okhotsk from Udskoi up to Okhotsk. South: the engraved dotted border of the Russian empire with its colour wash, against Tartary and Chinese Tartary; this side is clear. West: the yellow outline of Russian Asia along the Ural chain, then a line just west of the first letter R down to the Tartary border.

lands.name: TARTARY
lands.note: North: the engraved dotted border with red and yellow wash against Russian Asia, from the Jemba to the Altay. East: the dotted border with red and green wash against Chinese Tartary, round the tongue of land at Hami down to the Gobi. South: from the Gobi west to Cashmir a dotted line that I read as the north limit of Tibet, then the dotted border with red wash against Hindoostan (Cabul) and Persia. West: the border against Corasan and the east shore of the Caspian. The pink body colour does not stop at the Tibet line: it runs on over Tibet as one wash, and the last letter Y of TARTARY stands just south of the line, inside Tibet. Tibet has its own name in letters of equal rank, so it is left out here.

lands.name: CHINESE TARTARY
lands.note: An engraved dotted border with a green outline wash nearly all the way round, and an olive body colour. North: the border against Russian Asia from the Altay past Selinginsk and the Argun to the sea at Udskoi. East: the coast from the Uda past the mouth of the Amur to Corea. South: the border of Corea, the palisade round Leaotong, the Great Wall and the border of China round Ortos and down to Kokonor. West: the border against Tartary and Tibet. Ortos, Tangut and the Tartars of Kokonor are inside. Saghalien is outlined in the same green but is left out of the ring, as are the other islands.

lands.name: WESTERN
lands.note: The word WESTERN stands alone north of the Gobi and has no limit of its own; it marks the west half of Chinese Tartary. North, south and west sides are the border of Chinese Tartary. East: my own line, down the chain of hills drawn from Lake Kulon to the Great Wall, which passes between the last letter of CHINESE and the first of TARTARY. The sheet draws no boundary there.

lands.name: EASTERN

North, east and south sides are the border and coast of Chinese Tartary. West: my own line, down the chain of hills drawn from Lake Kulon to the Great Wall. The sheet draws no boundary there, and the name MONGALS is lettered on both sides of it.

maps.says: The word appears once on this sheet, spelled TATAREY, in seven capitals that run from the east shore of the Caspian across the Aral Sea to the mountains west of Kashgar. A red outline with a pink wash marks its ground: the Turkoman country, Charesm (Khiva), Turkestan, Fergana and GROSS BUCHAREY with Bukhara, Samarkand and Balkh. Everything north of that is lettered RUSSISCHES REICH with WEST-SIBIRIEN and OST SIBIRIEN, and the Kirghiz hordes sit on the Russian side of the line. To the east the old Chinese Tartary is gone: the sheet letters SOONGAREY, KALMUKEY, MONGOLEY, KLEINE BUCHAREY and TIBET, and the Manchu country carries its own province names with no Tartary at all.
doubts: The title block gives the date as 1805 after the words Nürnberg, bey Homanns Erben. A small word under the date looks like verbessert (improved), which would mean this is a corrected state of an older plate; I could not read it with full certainty. The library record also gives 1805.

The title was read from the title block at the bottom left; small words in it (den or de, Hrn) follow my reading and the library record where the engraving was hard to make out. The block ends with the privilege line Mit Röm. Kaiserl. allergn. Freyheit, which is left out of the title. The title block and the table of scales at the top right are cut out as holes and hold no Tartary wording that I saw.

TATAREY is the only lettering with the word that I found. I read the sheet at reading size across the band from the Black Sea to Japan and from the Arctic to north India; the far south (Arabia, south India, the islands) and the sea names were looked over at a smaller size, so a small Tartar name there could have been missed.

The Crimea is lettered Krim only, and the Manchu country shows province names (Tsitsikar, Kirin Ula) and Mandschu, with no Tatarey that I could find. The large spread capitals in the Manchu country overlap each other and I could not read every word there.
The limit of TATAREY is hand colour (a red outline and a pink wash). I could not make out an engraved dotted border under the red, so another copy of this map could be coloured differently.
A second red line inside the outline separates the Charesm and Turkoman part from Gross Bucharey. I treated both as one Tartary because the single word is spread across both.
The sheet draws the Aral Sea as a narrow strip between two red lines. The ring follows those lines, which makes a deep notch in the north-west of the land.
The second letter of TATAREY sits on the land between the Caspian and the Aral and is partly hidden by hill shading; I read it as A from the word as a whole.

The first worker's points west of about x 1300 and in the far south and east were found shifted on the check picture and were moved onto the town marks. Rome, Hamburg, Tornio and Bab el Mandeb still fit badly because they lie at the edge of the sheet, where the map's own projection bends most.
Kolyma mouth and Lena delta are marked skip: I was not sure which river mouth on that coast is which.
The Arctic coast east of the Taymyr and the far north-east are drawn from Russian surveys of the 1700s and fit the real coast only loosely.
Tashkent, Kashgar and Yarkand are each 150 to 190 km out when left out of the fit. Their marks were checked; the mapmaker's own positions for inner Asia are that rough.
The letter positions of KALMUKEY and of the larger MONGOLEY are approximate in the middle of each word.
The strait between the mainland and Sachalin was read closely for a Gulf of Tartary name: there is none, only notes on the little known coast and Jeso Land.
uncertain: The outline of Tartary here is hand colouring on this one copy. Another copy could be coloured differently.
The date 1805 is printed on the map, but a small word by it seems to say the plate was an improved reissue of older work.
We found the word only once on the sheet. A very small Tartar name in a corner we read less closely could have been missed.
The edges of the sheet (Europe, Arabia, the far north-east) sit less exactly on the real earth than the middle.
The mapmaker's own places in inner Asia are off by 100 to 200 km, so the outline on the modern map is only that exact.

maps.head: Two Tartarys under a Russian north
maps.title: ASIA According to the best AUTHORITIES.
maps.title_plain: Asia, according to the best authorities
maps.says: This American atlas sheet uses the word twice, as two bordered countries side by side: WESTERN TARTARY from the Caspian to the edge of the Kobi desert, and EASTERN TARTARY from there to the Sea of Korea, down to the Chinese Wall. Each has a dotted boundary line and its own outline colour. Inside them the sheet letters peoples and districts: Kalmucks, Turkistan, Usbecks and Karacalpacks in the west, Kalkas, Mongols, Daouria, Kitching and Mantcheou in the east. Everything north of the two is RUSSIAN EMPIRE and SIBERIA, with no Tartary in the name, and the only other use of the word is the small Kasatsha Horde Tartars on the steppe.
doubts: No date and no imprint are printed on the sheet. The year 1814 is the Library of Congress catalogue date, which goes with the 1814 issue of Carey's General Atlas (the sheet is numbered 51 at the top right). Carey used the same plate in earlier issues of the atlas too, so the engraving itself may be some years older.
The mapmaker's name is not on the sheet either; Carey is the publisher given by the catalogue.

The title is lettered in an oval at the top left, over Europe; it is cut out as a hole. The far north east of Siberia breaks through the top border of the map and the neat line is drawn round that bump.
The longitude scale along the bottom counts from Philadelphia and the one along the top from London.
Western Tartary: the limit is a dotted line and outline colour nearly all the way round. The odd narrow tongue up the Tobol to Tobolsk is as the sheet draws it. The west side is the Caspian shore.

Eastern Tartary: the boundary with Korea is my reading. Korea is outlined in the same pink as Eastern Tartary and there is no dotted line between them, so the ring follows the mountain chain drawn along Korea's north west side and comes out at the coast near Furdan.
The palisade country round Shinyang (Liaodong) is outlined green like China and is left out of Eastern Tartary.

Balkh is drawn west of Bukhara, though it really lies south east of it; Lake Zaysan is drawn about seven degrees too far east; Yaksa (Albazin) is drawn close to Nerchinsk. These are kept as the mapmaker's own errors and fit badly (250 to 400 km).
North east Siberia, Sakhalin and Japan are drawn from thin reports and fit badly (Cape Dezhnev, Anadyr mouth, Cape Chelyuskin, north tip of Sakhalin, north tip of Honshu about 250 to 350 km).
The far corners of the sheet (Cape Guardafui, Suez, Constantinople, Malacca, Ceylon) have few places near them and fit loosely; they lie outside the dial frame.
A river in north east Siberia lettered something like Tjandina could be the Chondon or the Indigirka; it is recorded but left out of the fit.

Yakutsk and Constantinople have no clear town mark; they are placed on the river and on the strait beside the name. The Amur is not drawn clearly to the sea, so its mouth is placed at the notch in the coast opposite Sagalin.
MANTCHEOU is lettered in small open capitals that cross the word TARTARY; the reading of its middle letters is not certain.
The engraver cut Bokaia for Bokhara, Bagdal for Bagdad and Hashgar for Kashgar.
uncertain: The sheet has no printed date. 1814 is the library's date for the atlas it comes from, and the plate may be a little older.
Both Tartarys have a dotted border line and a colour outline, so their limits are clear, except where Eastern Tartary meets Korea: there the line is my reading of a mountain chain.
The mapmaker put several inner Asian places well out of position (Balkh, Lake Zaysan, Albazin), so the bent sheet is off by a few hundred kilometres in places.
North east Siberia, Sakhalin and Japan were poorly known and sit badly on the real coast.

maps.title_plain: Asia, drawn under the direction of Mr Pinkerton by L. Hebert, engraved by Neele of 352 Strand (London), published by Dobson, Philadelphia
maps.says: Pinkerton spells the word Tatary, without the first R, and uses it three times. Independent Tatary lies over the Kirghiz steppe and Bukhara, Chinese Tatary runs in one long line from Khotan through Mongolia and Mandshuria to the Amur, and the strait beside Sakhalin is the Channel of Tatary. North of them there is no Russian Tatary at all: the whole north is Siberia, divided into Russian governments.
doubts: Earlier notes gave the spelling as TARTARY; on the sheet each of the three names has six letters, T A T A R Y.
The last word of CHANNEL OF TATARY is small and lies over sea shading; it is read as TATARY by its letter count and by the map's own spelling elsewhere.
The far north was searched strip by strip: no Russian, Muscovite or Siberian Tatary is lettered, only SIBERIA and the governments of Tobolsk, Irkutsk and so on.
The second line of hollow capitals for CHINESE EMPIRE (EMPIRE, across Tibet and China) is not outlined; only its first word is recorded in also.
SIBERIA and MANDSHURIA are followed letter by letter among other spaced government names, so one or two of their letter positions may belong to a neighbouring name.
East Cape, the Lena delta, the Aral Sea centre and the southern tip of Novaya Zemlya are placed by eye on drawn coasts and are good to about 50 sheet pixels.

Lands: the hand colour gives Independent Tatary a pale pink body that runs south without a break over Balk, Cabul and Cashmir to the Hindostan line. The lettering stops near Bukhara. No engraved line or second country name divides the south, so the ring follows the colour; a reader could as well stop it at the Ghurhead (Hindu Kush) chain near y 3300.
Lands: Candahar is washed green with Persia while Cabul is pink; that split is the colourist's and the engraved dotted Persian line agrees with it.

Lands: the blue-green wash meant for the Chinese side also fills the Russian governments of KOLYVAN and NERTCHINSK, with the yellow Russian outline drawn north of them. Both are lettered as Russian governments, so the Chinese Tatary ring keeps to the engraved dotted line and the mountain chains instead.
Lands: between Bouktarminsk and the yellow line at about x 4700 the limit is taken along the Sayansk Mountains chain; only a short piece of dotted line is visible there (x 4120 to 4230).

Lands: between Kiakta and the Argun the ring follows a faint dotted line past the frontier forts (x 5300 to 5700, y 2240 to 2290); it may be a road and not the frontier, and is good to about 40 sheet pixels.

Lands: the sheet draws no limit between Chinese Tatary and Tibet; the blue outline goes round both together. The ring's south-west side (y about 3400 to 3430, then north-east past Koko Nor to the Chinese line near Sining) is a judgement from the lettering and the edge of the Cobi desert.

Lands: Corea is washed blue like the outline of Chinese Tatary but is lettered as its own country and has a dotted line on its west side; it is left out. Its northern edge (y about 2780 to 2815) is taken from where the blue body wash begins and is approximate. Leaotong, also blue and outside the Great Wall, is kept inside Chinese Tatary.
Lands: Sagalin (Tchoka) island is washed blue-green like the Chinese side but lies beyond the Channel of Tatary and is not traced.

Second look for lettering: the sheet north of y 4600 was read again tile by tile at full size (except the open sea east of Japan and inner Arabia); no further Tartar or Tatar lettering was found. Crimea is lettered CRIMEA only; no Little Tatary.

lands.name: INDEPENDENT TATARY
lands.note: Follows the pale pink body wash and its darker pink edge line. North and north-west: the engraved dotted line of the Russian Empire under the yellow outline, from the Caspian near the Emba up to Omsk. East: the Irtysh line down to Bouktarminsk, then the edge of the blue Chinese wash round the Lake Palkati lobe, out along the wedge toward Golza, and down the Belur Tag to Cashmir. South: the pink runs on without a break over Balk, Cabul and Cashmir to the yellow line of Hindostan; no line or second name parts these from the rest, though the lettering itself stops near Bukhara. South-west: the dotted line and green wash of Persia. West: the Caspian shore.

lands.name: CHINESE TATARY
lands.note: Follows the blue-green outline wash of the Chinese lands outside China, corrected by the engraved lines. West: the edge shared with Independent Tatary along the Belur Tag and the Lake Palkati lobe. North: the engraved dotted line and mountain chains (Sayansk Mountains, the line of posts from Kiakta to the Argun, the Argun, the Daourian or Stannovoi chain to the Ouda); the colourist's blue also covers the Russian governments of Kolyvan and Nertchinsk, which are left out here. East: the coast along the Channel of Tatary and the Sea of Japan; the island of Sagalin, also washed blue, is left out. South-east: the edge of Corea and the coast of Leaotong, then the pink line of China along the Great Wall. South-west, toward Tibet: the sheet draws no limit and the same blue outline runs on round Tibet, so the ring is drawn by the lettering, along the south edge of the Cobi desert about halfway to the name TIBET.

maps.says: On this sheet Chinese Tartary is a name of the title only. Across the map body the country beyond the Great Wall is lettered by its peoples instead: the Country of the Kalmuks or Eleuths, the Country of the Kalkas, the Mongols, and in Manchuria the Taguri, Solons, Yupi and Keching. The one place the word itself appears on the land is small: TARTARS of Kogo Nor, beside the lake of Koko Nor.
doubts: No TARTARY lettering was found on the map body. The large spaced-out lettering near the top reads COUNTRY of the KALMUKS or ALUTHS and COUNTRY of the KALKAS, not Tartary. The whole sheet was read at half scale and the belt north of China at full close views; the print is faint, so a very small Tartar word could have been missed.
Mongolia, Manchuria (Mantchooria), Soongaria and Tibet are not lettered in English as region names; Tibet, Mongolia and the Manchu provinces appear only in Chinese characters.

West of Kashgar the map is laid down from 'Oriental geographers', not survey: the Caspian, Aral, Samarkand and Balkhash points are true places badly placed, so the fit is poor there. The rivers taken as the Volga and the Ural are unnamed.
Lake Baikal and Lhasa could not be used: Baikal is not drawn and no town symbol could be tied to Lhasa with confidence.
Sakhalin is drawn as a small island off the Amur mouth and was not used as a fitting point.
The Seoul, Selenginsk and Ussuri points rest on small unlabelled symbols or junctions.

maps.head: Independent Tartary, already shared out
maps.title: PERSIA, ARABIA, TARTARY, AFGHANISTAN
maps.title_plain: Persia, Arabia, Tartary, Afghanistan
maps.says: The word stands twice on this sheet. It is one of the four countries named in the title, and across the steppe the mapmaker spreads INDEPENDENT TARTARY in two long lines, the first from the north Caspian to Lake Balkhash and the second from the Karakum desert past Khiva and Bukhara to the Pamir, all inside one green border that runs from the Ural river round to the Hindu Kush. Inside that border the land is already shared out under other names, Kirguis Country with its three hordes, Turkestan, Kowaresmia and Great Bucharia, while Siberia, Soongaria and Little Bucharia lie outside it.
doubts: The title has no cartouche; it is lettered across the empty north-west corner of the map body, so its TARTARY is recorded as a label.
The north-east corner is the weakest part of the fit: Kashgar, Lake Balkhash and Issyk Kul are drawn from thin report and sit 150 to 300 km from their true places.
Khiva and the lower Amu, and the interior of Afghanistan and Belochistan (Kandahar, Kalat), are 200 km or so out on the sheet itself.
The south-east corner is open sea with no places to match; the nearest are Cambay, Karachi, Ras al Hadd and Socotra.
Letter heights and the ends of the small curved names (KOWARESMIA, TURKESTAN, TURCOMANIA) are read to within about 10 pixels on a small scan.
The smaller names KHIEVA, FERGANA, ALSHASH, OSRUSHNA, SOGD, KOTLAN and TOKARESTAN inside Independent Tartary, and LITTLE THIBET and KAUSHKAR outside it, are on the sheet but not listed in also.

TARTARY in the title and INDEPENDENT TARTARY on the map are treated as one land: the title word has no lettering, border or colour of its own on the map, and the only Tartary the sheet draws is the green-bordered Independent Tartary.

The limit of Independent Tartary is the green hand colour. It rests on engraved features for most of the way (the Ural river, a dotted line from Orskaia to the Ula Tau, the mountain chains on the north and east, the Tedzen river, the Caspian shore), but from the Indus at Draus west to Balkh and on to Meroo al Rood the green has no engraved line under it and runs only beside the pink Afghan border.

The green takes in KAUSHKAR and CAUFIRISTAN OR KUTTORE, down to the Indus at Draus. An engraved dotted line parts Caufiristan from Kaushkar, so the engraver may have meant Caufiristan to lie outside; the ring follows the colour here because no lettering contradicts it.
Near Meroo al Rood, where the green, the yellow Persian and the pink Afghan colours meet, the green breaks for about 80 pixels; the corner of the ring there (about 2530, 2035) is joined by eye.
The same green also outlines Arabia on this copy. The two outlines do not touch, so it is read as the colourist using one green twice, not as one country.

The west side follows the drawn Caspian shore; the gulfs on the north-east shore (Gulf of Emba, Dead Gulf, the peninsula lettered Gulf of T. Karasson) are traced in simplified form, to within about 10 pixels.
Lake Balkhash is drawn outside the green border, east of the mountain chain, so the ring leaves it out.

The sheet was searched again at reading size from the north edge to the Persian Gulf and the Indus for Tartar lettering; none was found beyond the three labels. Arabia south of the Tropic and the African shore were checked on the whole-sheet view only.
The Uralsk point was moved about 27 pixels onto the town circle; it had been set on the river bend beside it.

lands.name: INDEPENDENT TARTARY
lands.note: One land: the two lines INDEPENDENT and TARTARY are a single name, and the TARTARY of the title has no ground of its own apart from it. The ring follows the green outline colour, which closes all the way round. North: the green runs up the Ural river from its mouth to Uralsk and east along the river past Orenburg to Orskaia, then along an engraved dotted line and the Ula Tau and Algydim Shalo mountains, with SIBERIA lettered beyond. East: the green follows the engraved mountain chain west of Lake Balkhash, past L. Tuscul and down the Beloor Tag, leaving Balkash L., Cashgar, SOONGARIA, LITTLE BUCHARIA and LITTLE THIBET outside. South: the green follows a dotted line and mountains north of KAUSHKAR to the Indus at Draus, turns back west beside the pink Afghan border under CAUFIRISTAN and Balkh, then runs north-west past Meroo Shajean and along the Tedzen or Ochus river beside the yellow Persian border to the Caspian at the Balkan Bay. West: the Caspian shore as the sheet draws it, with its gulfs (Dead Gulf, Gulf of Emba), back to the Ural mouth.

maps.head: One modest line by the Aral Sea
maps.title: ASIA.
maps.title_plain: Asia (plate 63 of S. Augustus Mitchell, A New Universal Atlas, Philadelphia 1849; no imprint is lettered on the sheet itself)
maps.says: By 1849 the word Tartary has shrunk to one modest line of spaced capitals in central Asia, running from just west of the Sea of Aral across Khokan to the edge of Soongaria, with no border or colour of its own. It is threaded among the names that have taken its place: Turcomania, Khiva, Great Bucharia, Khokan, Kirguis and Turkestan. Farther east the sheet letters Soongaria, Mongolia, Little Bucharia, Mandshuria and Chinese Empire with no Chinese Tartary at all, and the only other survival is the small Channel of Tartary between Saghalin and the mainland.
doubts: The third letter of TARTARY (the first R) falls inside the wave shading of the Sea of Aral and can hardly be seen; the word is read from the other six letters, which are evenly spaced along one line.
TARTARY is no larger than TURCOMANIA beside it (capitals about 22 pixels high) and much smaller than RUSSIA, SIBERIA or CHINESE EMPIRE.

The list of other names is capped at eight, taken by size of lettering. Left out for the cap: TURKESTAN (running on from the end of TARTARY toward Little Bucharia), GR. BUCHARIA, KHIVA, KHOKAN, SOONGARIA, KALKAS, and the Russian government names TOBOLSK, IRKOUTSK, OKHOTSK, KOLHYVANE, with the peoples SAMOYEDS and TOUNGOOSI.

RUSSIA and SIBERIA cross each other and the government name IRKOUTSK in eastern Siberia; their last two letters (I, A) were told apart by letter style (RUSSIA in open shaded capitals, SIBERIA in solid ones).
No imprint, date or publisher line is lettered on this sheet; only the title ASIA. and the plate number 63 in the lower right margin. The atlas title and date come from the catalogue.
Kashgar is the worst place in the fit (about 450 km): the sheet draws it too far north-west, against Khokan. Samarcand is also set too near Bokhara. Both are kept because their identity is certain.
The south-east corner (Guam, Palau, Yap) and the south-west corner (Aden, Cape Guardafui) fit less well, 250 to 400 km when left out, mostly because few places hold the sheet there.
The map body was searched at full size in twelve strips for any Tartar lettering; only the two labels recorded were found. Very small italic names in the hatching of the seas could still hide a word.
No matched places were set south of about 5 degrees north or in the Australia inset, so the bend is not to be trusted there.

TARTARY has no border and no colour of its own. Its letters stand in Turcomania (green), in the Sea of Aral, in Khokan (yellow) and in the south-east corner of Kirguis (pink); each of those is coloured as a separate state, and the colours of Turcomania and Great Bucharia happen to be the same green.

The land ring is a reading of the lettering, not a drawn limit: it follows the outer engraved and coloured borders of the five small states between the Caspian, Russia, the Chinese Empire, Persia and Afghanistan (Kirguis, Turcomania, Khiva, Khokan, Great Bucharia). The sheet never says in words that these five make up Tartary.

Khiva and Great Bucharia are not touched by any letter of TARTARY; they were taken in because they lie between the lettering and the larger names PERSIA and AFGHANISTAN. A narrower reading would leave them out.

All of Kirguis was taken in, north to its border near Verkho Ouralsk, although only the last two letters (R, Y) stand in its southern corner. This is the most generous part of the ring; a narrower reading would stop well south of that border.
TARTARY is lettered no larger than KIRGUIS or TURKESTAN, which overlap it, so it reads as a loose regional name laid over the states and not as a country of higher rank.

The south-east corner of the ring, from the end of the dotted mountain line at Mustooch round Chitral to the dotted Cabul border, was judged from a ridge and a river: the green of Great Bucharia and the grey-green of the Chinese Empire are hard to tell apart there.
The Caspian shore of the ring is simplified at the Karasou Gulf and the small bays north of it.
The fit is weak around Kashgar and Kabul, so the south-east part of the land (printed as covering parts of Afghanistan and Pakistan) lands less surely on today's earth than the rest.
A second look over the Black Sea, Russia, Siberia, Mongolia, Mandshuria and the Pacific coast found no further Tartar lettering.

maps.head: One plain Tartary, east of the Caspian
maps.by: Harper and Brothers, New York; engraved by Charles Copley, New York
maps.title: ASIA
maps.title_plain: Asia
maps.says: The word TARTARY is lettered once, in plain capitals with no Independent or Chinese in front of it, from the east shore of the Caspian across the Aral Sea to just short of Lake Balkhan (Balkhash). No border is drawn round it and the sheet has no colour; inside it sit KHIVA, BOKHARA, KOKAN, Turcomania and the Kirghiz hordes. The north is RUSSIAN EMPIRE and SIBERIA, and the ground older maps called Chinese Tartary is now CHINESE EMPIRE with MONGOLIA, MANTCHOORIA, TCHOONGORIA and THIAN CHAN NANLOO. Elsewhere the word survives only in small things: the G. of Tartary beside Sagalian, a people called Tartars near Tomsk, and two place names, Tatarsk and Tatar.
doubts: No date is printed anywhere on the sheet. The lower margin carries only HARPER & BROTHERS, NEW YORK. and Engraved by Charles Copley, N. York, with no copyright line. The year 1855 rests on the Library of Congress catalogue alone, which itself gives both 1855 and [1850?].
The sheet may come from a Harper gazetteer or atlas of the 1850s, but nothing on the sheet says so and this was not checked.

The sheet is uncoloured and has no key. Thin wavy lines are province and country limits in Russia, but east of the Caspian the wavy lines are mostly rivers, and I could not always tell a limit from a river. The broken (dashed) lines near the R. Tchoui and R. Sari-Sou are taken to be rivers that lose themselves in the steppe, not borders.

TARTARY has no drawn limit. Its ring is my reading: the largest doubt is the north side, where I kept the Kirghiz Little and Middle Hordes inside and carried the ring to the Russian frontier (the Oural river and the dotted line south of OMSK province). A narrower reading would stop near the Aral Sea and the Syr-deria and give a much smaller land.
Between Orsk and the hills near Lake Naourzoum the sheet draws no frontier, and the ring runs straight across.
The dotted line from the Attruck past Mushed towards Herat is taken as the frontier of Persia; it could be a road.
On the east the ring passes west of Lake Balkhan and Kashgar by judgement; the sheet draws no line between TARTARY and the Chinese Empire there.
Lake Balkhan (Balkhash) is drawn as a small lake standing north to south, about 450 km from where the fit expects it; it is recorded but left out of the fit.

The far north-east fits worst (East Cape about 310 km, C. North about 200 km, Oust Iansk about 190 km): the Arctic coast east of the Lena is stretched on the sheet and these points lie at the edge. Matochkin Strait in Nova Zembla (about 200 km) and North Cape of Norway (about 180 km) also sit at the edge of the sheet.
Mocha and Manila fit poorly (about 170 and 150 km); both are at the south edge, outside the dial frame.
Tatarsk (a town on the Irtish) and Tatar (a village on the lower Amour) are recorded as labels of family other; they are place names, not countries.
The reading Turcomania, in spaced italic down the east side of the Caspian, is not certain; the last letters are faint and it may read Turcomans.
The name read TCHOONGORIA is spread among other lettering (OR THIAN CHAN PELOO) and the first letters are not certain.
The last two letters of SIBERIA, east of the Lena, were placed by estimate among the letters of IAKOUTSK.
No Tartar name was found in the Crimea, the Caucasus, Mongolia or Manchuria; I searched the whole sheet in strips at reading size.
The title box ASIA and a Library of Congress stamp at the upper left are cut out as holes. At the upper right the map breaks through the border to show Bhering Strait and a corner of North America.
uncertain: The sheet has no printed date. About 1855 comes from the library catalogue, which also says it could be about 1850.
The map draws no border round Tartary and has no colour, so the outline shown is our reading of where the word reaches.
The north side is the biggest guess: we kept the Kirghiz steppe inside Tartary, up to the Russian frontier. A narrower reading would make the land much smaller.
On the east side nothing on the map separates Tartary from the Chinese Empire; we drew the line along the mountains near Kashgar.
Two small names, Tatarsk and Tatar, are a town and a village, not countries.

maps.head: The country is gone; a people and a gulf keep the word
maps.title: JOHNSON'S ASIA BY JOHNSON AND WARD.
maps.title_plain: Johnson's Asia, by Johnson and Ward (no imprint line is lettered on the sheet; plate number 82 in the corner)
maps.says: On this American family atlas sheet of 1862 the country called Tartary is gone. Where older maps spread that name, this one letters TOORKISTAN with Khiva, Bokhara and Khokand, and Siberia, Outer and Inner Mongolia and Manchooria, all inside the Russian Empire and the Chinese Empire. The word survives in only two small places: KIRGHIZ TARTARS, the name of a people on the steppe north of the Aral Sea, and the Gulf of Tartary, the water between Saghalin and the mainland.
doubts: Search for the Tartar word: the whole map body inside the neat line was read on close views in overlapping strips about 660 sheet pixels wide (x 290 to 4610, y 190 to 3600), row by row from the Arctic coast to the bottom edge, with a second closer look at the Kirghiz steppe, Toorkistan, Mongolia, Manchooria, the Amoor and Saghalin. Only two letterings hold the word: KIRGHIZ TARTARS (two lines, a people) and Gulf of Tartary (a water). Nothing else turned up: no Tartary, Chinese Tartary, Independent Tartary or Crim Tartary anywhere, on land or sea. One small patch of open Pacific near the right edge (x 4310 to 4610, y 3120 to 3280) was seen only on the reduced check picture; it holds no lettering.

The names that stand where Tartary used to be, confirmed on close views: TOORKISTAN in large capitals, with KHIVA, BOKHARA and KHOKAND in smaller spaced capitals inside it and TOORKOMANIA beside the Caspian; SIBERIA and RUSSIAN EMPIRE in long arcs; OUTER MONGOLIA, INNER MONGOLIA, MANCHOORIA, CHINESE EMPIRE and BOD OR TIBET. The eight largest are in 'also'; the three khanates and the Siberian provinces (TOBOLSK, TOMSK, IENISEISK, IRKOUTSK, IAKOUTSK, OKHOTSK) are smaller and left out.

The last A of SIBERIA is taken as the capital A at about (3727, 684), among the letters of the province name OKHOTSK; the letters of SIBERIA, RUSSIAN EMPIRE, IAKOUTSK and OKHOTSK cross each other in east Siberia, so the east end of the SIBERIA outline is the least certain of the outlines.

No imprint or copyright line is lettered on this sheet; the title block reads JOHNSON'S ASIA BY JOHNSON AND WARD and the corner carries the plate number 82. The place and date (New York, 1862) come from the library record, not from the sheet.

Fit: 80 places, north of about 5 degrees north, reaching all four sides. Most land within 100 km. The poorest are at the edges: East Cape and North East Cape on the Arctic rim, the north tip of Nova Zembla, the Kolyma mouth, and Aden in the south-west corner; Lake Balkhash and Khokand are simply misplaced by the mapmaker. All were re-read on close views and kept.
The sheet runs south to about 5 degrees south (Sumatra, Borneo, New Guinea); no places were matched south of Ceylon, so the bend is not held there.

Kirghiz Tartars lettering is very small (capitals about 13 sheet pixels high) and Gulf of Tartary is small italic (about 22); both outlines were checked against the lettering on cut pieces of the check picture.

maps.head: Only the water remembers
maps.title: ASIEN.
maps.title_plain: Asia
maps.says: The word Tartary is gone from the land on this German atlas map. The only trace is a small name in the water between the mainland and Sakhalin, Tatar'scher Golf, the Tartar Gulf. Where older maps wrote Tartary, this one writes Russisches Reich and Chinesisches Reich in big spaced letters, with West-Sibirien, Ost-Sibirien, Turkestan, Ost-Turkestan, Mongolei and Mandschurei beneath them.
doubts: Maker and date: the sheet itself carries 'Verlag R. Grossmann, Berlin S.W. 29.' under the lower right corner, 'Red. O. Brunckow, Berlin.' under the lower left, 'Alle Rechte vorbehalten.' twice, and page numbers 50. and 51. at the top corners. No year is printed anywhere on the sheet. The 1894 date rests on the Library of Congress catalogue entry for the atlas, not on the sheet. The content agrees with a date around then: the colour key has 'Deutsche Schutzherrschaft', Kaiser Wilhelms Land is on New Guinea, Burma is in the British colour, Wladiwostok is lettered, and no Siberian railway is drawn.

Title as lettered in the block at the lower left: 'ASIEN.' with 'Maßstab 1:30 000.000.' beneath it. The small inset is headed 'Völkerkarte von ASIEN. Auf Grundlage v. Friedr. Müller's "Allgem. Ethnographie" nach v. Haardt, Gerland u. A.'

Search for the Tartar word: the whole map body was read on close views, in sixteen overlapping pieces from x 1400 to 6025 and y 300 to 3800 (four rows of four, each about 1250 by 950 sheet pixels), then three pieces down the west side (x 290 to 1540, Europe, the Mediterranean and north-east Africa with the title block), three along the south edge (y 3750 to 4350), the top and bottom margins, and tighter views of the Volga and Crimea, the Kirgisen-Steppe and Turkestan, East Turkestan, Mongolia, Manchuria, the Amur and Sakhalin. The only lettering found with the word is 'Tatar'scher Golf' beside Sakhalin. Nothing else turned up: no Tartarei, Tatarei or Tataren on land anywhere, including the Crimea, the Volga and Kazan country, and the steppe.

The ethnographic inset (x 390 to 1810, y 3140 to 4180) and its key were read on close views. Its key lists Papua's & Melanesier, Afrik. Neger, Australier, Arktiker & Hyperboreer, Malayen & Polynesier, Dravida's, Mongolen (mit einsilb. Spr., mit mehrsilb. Spr.) and Mittelländer (Basken, Kaukasier, Hamito-Semiten, Indo-Europäer). There is no Tataren in the key or on the inset. The inset's own land names are West-Sibirien, Ost-Sibirien, Turkestan, Ost-Turkestan, Mongolei, Mandschurei, Tibet, China, Iran, Arabien, Hindustan and so on.
'Tatar'scher Golf' is small italic lettering crossed by a meridian line and crowded by 'Constantinowsk'. The ending before Golf reads as r (Tatar'scher) but could be n.

Names that took Tartary's place: the eight in 'also' are the largest. RUSSISCHES REICH and CHINESISCHES REICH are each set on two lines, so each has two entries. Also lettered across the same country but left out of the eight: 'Kirgisen-Steppe' north of the Aral Sea and Lake Balkhash, TIBET, 'Gobi-Wüste (Schamo)', Buchara and Chiwa.

Fit: places are kept north of about 8 degrees north. A fold runs down the middle of the sheet near x 3120 and the two halves do not meet perfectly there. The worst places when left out are at the far corners (East Cape at Bering Strait, Aden, Manila, the Arctic capes), where the sheet's projection curves most and there are no neighbours beyond to hold the fit. Arkhangelsk, Obdorsk, Fu-san, the south tip of Kyushu and Manila were placed from the coast beside the name because no clear town ring could be made out.

uncertain: No year is printed anywhere on the sheet. It carries 'Verlag R. Grossmann, Berlin S.W. 29.' and 'Red. O. Brunckow, Berlin.', and the 1894 date rests on the Library of Congress catalogue entry for the atlas.

The content agrees with a date around then: the colour key has 'Deutsche Schutzherrschaft', Kaiser Wilhelms Land is on New Guinea, Burma is in the British colour, Wladiwostok is lettered, and no Siberian railway is drawn.
A search of the whole map body found no Tartarei, Tatarei or Tataren on land anywhere, including the Crimea, the Volga and Kazan country, and the steppe.
The small inset map of peoples ('Völkerkarte von ASIEN') was read as well. There is no Tataren in its key or on the inset itself.
'Tatar'scher Golf' is small italic lettering crossed by a meridian line and crowded by 'Constantinowsk'. The ending before Golf reads as r (Tatar'scher) but could be n.

A fold runs down the middle of the sheet and the two halves do not meet perfectly there. The fit is worst at the far corners (East Cape at Bering Strait, Aden, Manila, the Arctic capes), and Arkhangelsk, Obdorsk, Fu-san, the south tip of Kyushu and Manila were placed from the coast beside the name because no clear town ring could be made out.
